generation_notes: For narrative books, major_events_or_movements lists major events. For poetry, wisdom, prophecy, and letters, it lists major movements or sections instead of inventing events. key_figures lists the important people (and, in poetic or apocalyptic books, personified or symbolic figures, labeled as such) who act, speak, or are held up as examples in each book. Jesus is listed in the Gospels, Acts, Hebrews, and Revelation, where he appears as a character or is the subject of extended comparison.

books.name: Genesis
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Moses as part of the Pentateuch; many modern scholars understand the Pentateuch as having a complex compositional history.
books.original_audience: Israel, especially as a people seeking to understand its origins and covenant identity.
books.purpose: To explain beginnings—creation, humanity, sin, nations, and Israel's patriarchal family—and to establish the covenant story that shapes the rest of Scripture.
books.historical_context: Genesis is set in the ancient Near East and moves from primeval history to the family stories of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Precise dates for many events are uncertain.
books.overall_theme: God creates, humanity rebels, and God continues His plan of blessing and restoration through covenant.
books.plain_english_summary: Genesis begins with creation, shows the spread of sin, and then narrows to one family through whom God promises blessing. The book ends with Jacob's family in Egypt because Joseph's rise to power preserves them during famine.

major_events_or_movements.title: Creation and the Fall
major_events_or_movements.description: God creates the world and humanity; Adam and Eve disobey, bringing sin and its consequences into the human story.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Flood and Noah
major_events_or_movements.description: Human violence and corruption lead to judgment by flood, while Noah's family is preserved and receives a covenant sign.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Patriarchs and Joseph
major_events_or_movements.description: God calls Abraham and continues covenant promises through Isaac and Jacob; Joseph eventually rises in Egypt and preserves the family during famine.

key_figures.name: Adam and Eve
key_figures.description: The first humans, created in God's image, whose disobedience brings sin and death into the world.

key_figures.name: Noah
key_figures.description: A righteous man preserved with his family through the flood, with whom God makes a covenant.

key_figures.name: Abraham
key_figures.description: Called by God to leave Ur and Haran; receives the covenant promises of land, offspring, and blessing to the nations.

key_figures.name: Sarah
key_figures.description: Abraham's wife, who bears Isaac in her old age as the child of promise.

key_figures.name: Isaac
key_figures.description: The son of promise, nearly offered as a sacrifice; father of Jacob and Esau.

key_figures.name: Jacob (Israel)
key_figures.description: Isaac's son, renamed Israel after wrestling with God; his twelve sons become the tribes of Israel.

key_figures.name: Esau
key_figures.description: Jacob's twin brother, who trades away his birthright; ancestor of the Edomites.

key_figures.name: Joseph
key_figures.description: Jacob's favored son, sold into slavery by his brothers, who rises to power in Egypt and saves his family from famine.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians broadly agree on Genesis' foundational role, while differing on questions such as the literary form and chronology of Genesis 1-11.

books.name: Exodus
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Moses.
books.original_audience: Israel, especially the generation formed through deliverance from Egypt and covenant at Sinai.
books.purpose: To recount God's deliverance of Israel from slavery, the covenant at Sinai, and the establishment of worship centered on God's presence.
books.historical_context: Exodus is set against the background of Egypt and the ancient Near East. The exact date of the exodus is debated among scholars.
books.overall_theme: God redeems His people, forms them into a covenant community, and dwells among them.
books.plain_english_summary: Exodus tells how God rescues Israel from Egyptian slavery, leads them through the sea, gives His law at Sinai, and instructs them to build the tabernacle so His presence may dwell among them.

major_events_or_movements.title: Moses and the Exodus
major_events_or_movements.description: God calls Moses, confronts Pharaoh through plagues, and leads Israel out of Egypt.

major_events_or_movements.title: Covenant at Sinai
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel receives the Ten Commandments and enters covenant with God.

major_events_or_movements.title: Tabernacle and God's Presence
major_events_or_movements.description: God gives instructions for the tabernacle; after the golden calf crisis and covenant renewal, the tabernacle is built and God's glory fills it.

key_figures.name: Moses
key_figures.description: Israel's deliverer and lawgiver, called at the burning bush to lead the people out of Egypt.

key_figures.name: Aaron
key_figures.description: Moses' brother and spokesman, later appointed as Israel's first high priest.

key_figures.name: Pharaoh
key_figures.description: The unnamed king of Egypt who enslaves Israel and resists God's demand to let the people go.

key_figures.name: Miriam
key_figures.description: Moses' sister, a prophetess who leads the women in song after the crossing of the sea.

key_figures.name: Jethro
key_figures.description: Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian, who advises him to appoint judges to share the work.

key_figures.name: Joshua
key_figures.description: Moses' assistant, who leads Israel in battle against the Amalekites.

key_figures.name: Bezalel
key_figures.description: A craftsman filled with God's Spirit to oversee building the tabernacle and its furnishings.

books.interpretive_notes: Views differ on the historical dating and route of the exodus, but the book's theological emphasis on deliverance and covenant is central across Christian traditions.

books.name: Leviticus
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Moses.
books.original_audience: Israel, especially priests and the covenant community worshiping at the tabernacle.
books.purpose: To teach Israel how a holy God can dwell among a sinful people through sacrifice, priesthood, purity, and holy living.
books.historical_context: Leviticus is situated at Sinai after the tabernacle has been erected and before Israel departs for the promised land.
books.overall_theme: God is holy, and His people are called to approach Him rightly and reflect His holiness in worship and life.
books.plain_english_summary: Leviticus explains sacrifices, priestly duties, clean and unclean categories, the Day of Atonement, and covenant holiness. It connects worship with ethical living.

major_events_or_movements.title: Sacrificial Instructions
major_events_or_movements.description: The book opens with regulations for offerings that structure Israel's worship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Priesthood Established
major_events_or_movements.description: Aaron and his sons are ordained; Nadab and Abihu die after offering unauthorized fire.

major_events_or_movements.title: Day of Atonement and Holiness
major_events_or_movements.description: The annual Day of Atonement is prescribed, followed by laws calling Israel to holy living.

key_figures.name: Moses
key_figures.description: Receives God's instructions at the tent of meeting and conveys them to the people and priests.

key_figures.name: Aaron
key_figures.description: Ordained as high priest; offers sacrifices and leads the Day of Atonement ritual.

key_figures.name: Nadab and Abihu
key_figures.description: Aaron's sons, who die after offering unauthorized fire before the LORD.

key_figures.name: Eleazar and Ithamar
key_figures.description: Aaron's surviving sons, who continue the priestly service.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians differ on how Leviticus' ceremonial, dietary, and civil laws apply today; most read its sacrifices and priesthood as fulfilled in Christ (as Hebrews argues) while its call to holiness and love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) remains directly relevant.

books.name: Numbers
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Moses.
books.original_audience: Israel during the wilderness period.
books.purpose: To recount Israel's journey from Sinai toward Canaan, exposing repeated unbelief while showing God's continuing faithfulness.
books.historical_context: Numbers covers Israel's wilderness years between Sinai and the plains of Moab. Census lists frame the transition from one generation to the next.
books.overall_theme: Human unbelief brings consequences, yet God remains faithful to His covenant purposes.
books.plain_english_summary: Numbers follows Israel from preparation at Sinai through rebellion and wilderness wandering to a new generation ready to enter Canaan.

major_events_or_movements.title: Departure from Sinai
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel is counted, organized, and begins the journey toward the promised land.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Spies and Wilderness Judgment
major_events_or_movements.description: Most spies discourage the people, and Israel refuses to enter Canaan; that generation is sentenced to wander.

major_events_or_movements.title: New Generation on the Plains of Moab
major_events_or_movements.description: After further rebellions and victories, a second census marks the generation preparing to enter the land.

key_figures.name: Moses
key_figures.description: Leads Israel through the wilderness and intercedes for the people after repeated rebellions.

key_figures.name: Aaron
key_figures.description: High priest whose authority is confirmed by his budding staff; dies on Mount Hor.

key_figures.name: Miriam
key_figures.description: Moses' sister, who opposes his leadership and is struck with a skin disease; dies at Kadesh.

key_figures.name: Joshua and Caleb
key_figures.description: The two spies who urge Israel to trust God and enter Canaan, and the only adults of their generation allowed to enter.

key_figures.name: Korah
key_figures.description: A Levite who leads a rebellion against Moses and Aaron and is judged when the earth swallows the rebels.

key_figures.name: Balak
key_figures.description: King of Moab who hires Balaam to curse Israel.

key_figures.name: Balaam
key_figures.description: A foreign seer who is prevented from cursing Israel and instead pronounces blessings, including the oracle of a rising star.

key_figures.name: Phinehas
key_figures.description: Aaron's grandson, whose zeal stops a plague after Israel's idolatry at Peor.

books.interpretive_notes: The large census figures in Numbers have been understood in different ways, including as literal totals or as numbers using a different counting unit; the book's theological message about unbelief and God's faithfulness does not depend on resolving that question.

books.name: Deuteronomy
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Moses, with the closing account of his death understood as added by a later hand.
books.original_audience: The new generation of Israel preparing to enter Canaan.
books.purpose: To renew the covenant, restate God's law for a new generation, and call Israel to love and obey God in the land.
books.historical_context: The book is framed as Moses' final addresses on the plains of Moab before Israel crosses the Jordan.
books.overall_theme: Covenant faithfulness means loving God wholeheartedly and living in obedient loyalty to Him.
books.plain_english_summary: Moses reviews Israel's history, restates the law, explains covenant blessings and curses, commissions Joshua, and dies before Israel enters Canaan.

major_events_or_movements.title: Moses Reviews Israel's Journey
major_events_or_movements.description: Moses retells key events from Sinai to Moab, emphasizing lessons from unbelief.

major_events_or_movements.title: Covenant Law Restated
major_events_or_movements.description: The Ten Commandments and wider covenant instructions are given to the new generation.

major_events_or_movements.title: Covenant Renewal and Moses' Death
major_events_or_movements.description: Blessings, curses, final songs and blessings, Joshua's commissioning, and Moses' death close the book.

key_figures.name: Moses
key_figures.description: Delivers his final addresses on the plains of Moab, renewing the covenant before his death on Mount Nebo.

key_figures.name: Joshua
key_figures.description: Commissioned as Moses' successor to lead Israel into the land.

key_figures.name: Caleb
key_figures.description: Remembered for wholeheartedly following the LORD when the other spies discouraged Israel.

key_figures.name: Sihon and Og
key_figures.description: Amorite kings whose defeat is recalled as evidence of God's power to give Israel victory.

books.interpretive_notes: Many scholars connect Deuteronomy with the 'Book of the Law' found in Josiah's reign (2 Kings 22), while traditional views hold to Mosaic origins; either way, it is among the Old Testament books Jesus quotes most often.

books.name: Joshua
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Joshua, though the book likely includes later editorial material.
books.original_audience: Israel after Moses, entering and settling Canaan.
books.purpose: To recount Israel's entrance into the promised land, the distribution of territory, and the call to covenant faithfulness.
books.historical_context: Joshua follows Deuteronomy and is set during Israel's transition from wilderness life to settlement in Canaan.
books.overall_theme: God is faithful to His promises, and His people are called to courageous, exclusive covenant loyalty.
books.plain_english_summary: Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan, through major campaigns, into tribal allotments, and finally calls the nation to choose faithful service to the LORD.

major_events_or_movements.title: Crossing the Jordan and Jericho
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel enters Canaan and captures Jericho after crossing the Jordan.

major_events_or_movements.title: Conquest Campaigns
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel experiences both failure at Ai and later victories as major opposition is subdued.

major_events_or_movements.title: Land Allotment and Covenant Renewal
major_events_or_movements.description: The land is apportioned among tribes, and Joshua renews the covenant at Shechem.

key_figures.name: Joshua
key_figures.description: Moses' successor, who leads Israel across the Jordan, through the conquest, and in covenant renewal at Shechem.

key_figures.name: Rahab
key_figures.description: A Canaanite woman of Jericho who hides the Israelite spies and is spared with her family.

key_figures.name: Achan
key_figures.description: Takes devoted plunder from Jericho, causing Israel's defeat at Ai.

key_figures.name: Caleb
key_figures.description: One of the faithful spies, who at eighty-five claims Hebron as his inheritance.

key_figures.name: The Gibeonites
key_figures.description: A Canaanite people who deceive Israel into making a peace treaty.

key_figures.name: Adoni-zedek
key_figures.description: King of Jerusalem who leads a coalition of kings against Gibeon and Israel.

key_figures.name: Eleazar
key_figures.description: The high priest who helps Joshua distribute the land among the tribes.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians differ in how they interpret the conquest narratives ethically and historically; the text presents the conquest as divine judgment and covenant fulfillment.

books.name: Judges
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; Jewish tradition has sometimes associated it with Samuel.
books.original_audience: Israel during the period between Joshua and the monarchy.
books.purpose: To explain Israel's recurring cycle of apostasy, oppression, crying out, and deliverance, while showing the need for faithful leadership.
books.historical_context: The book depicts a decentralized tribal society in Canaan before Israel had a king.
books.overall_theme: When God's people abandon covenant faithfulness, disorder deepens; God repeatedly shows mercy through deliverers.
books.plain_english_summary: Judges tells a downward spiral: Israel turns from God, suffers oppression, cries out, and is rescued by judges. The book becomes increasingly dark and ends with social and moral chaos.

major_events_or_movements.title: Early Cycles of the Judges
major_events_or_movements.description: Figures such as Othniel, Ehud, and Deborah deliver Israel from oppressors.

major_events_or_movements.title: Gideon and Jephthah
major_events_or_movements.description: Later judges show both God's deliverance and the growing flaws of Israel's leaders.

major_events_or_movements.title: Samson and National Disorder
major_events_or_movements.description: Samson's troubled judgeship is followed by stories of idolatry, violence, and civil war.

key_figures.name: Othniel
key_figures.description: Caleb's nephew and the first judge, who delivers Israel from a Mesopotamian king.

key_figures.name: Ehud
key_figures.description: A left-handed Benjaminite who assassinates Eglon, king of Moab.

key_figures.name: Deborah
key_figures.description: A prophetess and judge who summons Barak to lead Israel against the Canaanite army.

key_figures.name: Barak
key_figures.description: The military leader who defeats Sisera's forces alongside Deborah.

key_figures.name: Jael
key_figures.description: A Kenite woman who kills the fleeing commander Sisera.

key_figures.name: Gideon
key_figures.description: Called while hiding from the Midianites, he defeats them with only three hundred men.

key_figures.name: Abimelech
key_figures.description: Gideon's son, who seizes power by murdering his brothers and dies violently.

key_figures.name: Jephthah
key_figures.description: A rejected son who delivers Israel from the Ammonites but makes a tragic vow.

key_figures.name: Samson
key_figures.description: A Nazirite of great strength whose personal failings, including with Delilah, end in his capture and death among the Philistines.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpreters discuss how to evaluate the judges themselves, since the book often presents their flaws without comment; the repeated refrain that 'there was no king in Israel' frames the moral chaos of the closing chapters.

books.name: Ruth
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; Jewish tradition has sometimes associated it with Samuel.
books.original_audience: Israel, likely with special interest in David's ancestry and covenant faithfulness.
books.purpose: To show God's providence, loyal love, and the inclusion of a Moabite woman in the family line that leads to David.
books.historical_context: The story is set during the time of the judges, a period otherwise marked by instability and covenant failure.
books.overall_theme: God works through ordinary faithfulness, kindness, and providence to bring redemption.
books.plain_english_summary: Ruth follows Naomi and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth from grief and poverty to restoration. Ruth's loyalty leads to marriage with Boaz, and their family line becomes part of David's ancestry.

major_events_or_movements.title: Ruth Chooses Naomi and Israel's God
major_events_or_movements.description: After the deaths of their husbands, Ruth refuses to abandon Naomi and returns with her to Bethlehem.

major_events_or_movements.title: Ruth Meets Boaz
major_events_or_movements.description: Ruth gleans in Boaz's field and receives protection and kindness.

major_events_or_movements.title: Redemption and Family Restoration
major_events_or_movements.description: Boaz acts as kinsman-redeemer, marries Ruth, and their son Obed becomes grandfather of David.

key_figures.name: Naomi
key_figures.description: An Israelite widow who returns from Moab to Bethlehem in bitterness and is restored.

key_figures.name: Ruth
key_figures.description: Naomi's Moabite daughter-in-law, whose loyalty leads her to Bethlehem and into David's ancestry.

key_figures.name: Boaz
key_figures.description: A worthy relative of Naomi's family who acts as kinsman-redeemer and marries Ruth.

key_figures.name: Elimelech
key_figures.description: Naomi's husband, who moves the family to Moab during a famine and dies there.

key_figures.name: Orpah
key_figures.description: Naomi's other daughter-in-law, who returns to her own people in Moab.

key_figures.name: Obed
key_figures.description: The son of Ruth and Boaz; father of Jesse and grandfather of David.

books.interpretive_notes: Ruth's place in the canon varies: Christian Bibles place it after Judges, while the Hebrew Bible places it among the Writings, often read at the festival of Shavuot. Matthew 1:5 includes Ruth in Jesus' genealogy.

books.name: 1 Samuel
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; traditions connect material with Samuel, Nathan, and Gad, but the final form is later than Samuel's lifetime.
books.original_audience: Israel during the transition from judges to monarchy.
books.purpose: To recount the rise of the monarchy, the failure of Saul, and the emergence of David as God's chosen king.
books.historical_context: The book covers Israel's shift from tribal leadership to kingship amid Philistine pressure and internal spiritual decline.
books.overall_theme: God looks at the heart, resists proud leadership, and advances His purposes through faithful obedience.
books.plain_english_summary: 1 Samuel moves from Samuel's birth and prophetic ministry to Saul's rise and fall, then to David's anointing and long conflict with Saul.

major_events_or_movements.title: Samuel's Rise
major_events_or_movements.description: Samuel is born, called by God, and becomes a prophet and judge during a period of priestly corruption.

major_events_or_movements.title: Saul Becomes King and Fails
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel asks for a king; Saul is chosen but repeatedly disobeys God's commands.

major_events_or_movements.title: David's Rise
major_events_or_movements.description: David is anointed, defeats Goliath, and becomes Saul's rival while refusing to seize the throne by force.

key_figures.name: Hannah
key_figures.description: A barren woman who prays for a son, dedicates Samuel to the LORD, and sings a song of praise.

key_figures.name: Eli
key_figures.description: Priest at Shiloh, whose corrupt sons Hophni and Phinehas bring judgment on his household.

key_figures.name: Samuel
key_figures.description: Prophet, priest, and last judge of Israel, who anoints both Saul and David.

key_figures.name: Saul
key_figures.description: Israel's first king, who begins well but is rejected by God for disobedience.

key_figures.name: Jonathan
key_figures.description: Saul's son, a brave warrior and loyal friend to David.

key_figures.name: David
key_figures.description: A shepherd anointed as future king, who defeats Goliath and flees from Saul's jealousy.

key_figures.name: Goliath
key_figures.description: The Philistine champion from Gath defeated by David.

key_figures.name: Abigail
key_figures.description: A wise woman who prevents David from taking revenge on her foolish husband Nabal, and later becomes David's wife.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpreters differ on how to read Israel's request for a king, since the text presents kingship both as a rejection of God and as something God permits and uses; Samuel's warnings and God's choice of David hold both sides together.

books.name: 2 Samuel
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; built from royal and prophetic traditions.
books.original_audience: Israel under David's reign and later readers reflecting on the Davidic monarchy.
books.purpose: To narrate David's reign, God's covenant promise to his house, and the serious consequences of David's sin.
books.historical_context: The book is set during the consolidation of Israel's monarchy under David, with Jerusalem becoming the political and worship center.
books.overall_theme: God establishes David's dynasty, yet even the chosen king is accountable for sin and its consequences.
books.plain_english_summary: David becomes king over all Israel, captures Jerusalem, receives God's covenant promise, and experiences both great victories and deep family turmoil after his sin with Bathsheba.

major_events_or_movements.title: David Becomes King
major_events_or_movements.description: David is first king over Judah and then over all Israel; Jerusalem becomes his capital.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Davidic Covenant
major_events_or_movements.description: God promises David an enduring dynasty and future royal line.

major_events_or_movements.title: David's Sin and Family Crisis
major_events_or_movements.description: David's adultery and arranged killing are followed by conflict, rebellion, and grief within his household.

key_figures.name: David
key_figures.description: Becomes king over Judah and then all Israel, receives God's covenant promise, but sins grievously with Bathsheba.

key_figures.name: Ish-bosheth
key_figures.description: Saul's son, set up as a rival king over Israel before his assassination.

key_figures.name: Joab
key_figures.description: Commander of David's army, effective but often ruthless.

key_figures.name: Mephibosheth
key_figures.description: Jonathan's disabled son, to whom David shows covenant kindness.

key_figures.name: Bathsheba
key_figures.description: Wife of Uriah, taken by David; later mother of Solomon.

key_figures.name: Uriah the Hittite
key_figures.description: A loyal soldier whom David arranges to have killed in battle.

key_figures.name: Nathan
key_figures.description: The prophet who delivers the Davidic covenant and later confronts David's sin with a parable.

key_figures.name: Absalom
key_figures.description: David's son, who kills his brother Amnon and later leads a rebellion against his father.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians widely read the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7 as pointing toward Jesus as the Son of David, while also recognizing its immediate fulfillment in Solomon and David's dynasty.

books.name: 1 Kings
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; often understood as part of a larger historical work compiled from earlier royal records and prophetic sources.
books.original_audience: Judah and Israel, especially readers reflecting on the monarchy and exile.
books.purpose: To explain the history of the united and divided kingdoms in light of covenant faithfulness and failure.
books.historical_context: The book begins with Solomon and the temple, then describes the kingdom's division and the early kings of Israel and Judah.
books.overall_theme: The health of the kingdom is measured by loyalty to the LORD; idolatry and disobedience lead toward judgment.
books.plain_english_summary: Solomon builds the temple but later compromises through idolatry. After his death the kingdom divides, and prophetic voices such as Elijah confront royal unfaithfulness.

major_events_or_movements.title: Solomon's Reign and Temple
major_events_or_movements.description: Solomon receives wisdom, builds the temple, and reaches great prosperity.

major_events_or_movements.title: Kingdom Divides
major_events_or_movements.description: Solomon's later idolatry is followed by the split between Israel in the north and Judah in the south.

major_events_or_movements.title: Elijah Confronts Ahab
major_events_or_movements.description: Elijah challenges Baal worship and the policies of Ahab and Jezebel.

key_figures.name: Solomon
key_figures.description: David's son and successor, renowned for wisdom, who builds the temple but later turns to idolatry.

key_figures.name: Adonijah
key_figures.description: David's son, who attempts to seize the throne before Solomon is crowned.

key_figures.name: The Queen of Sheba
key_figures.description: A foreign ruler who visits Solomon to test his wisdom and praises Israel's God.

key_figures.name: Rehoboam
key_figures.description: Solomon's son, whose harsh policy prompts the northern tribes to break away.

key_figures.name: Jeroboam
key_figures.description: First king of the northern kingdom, who sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan.

key_figures.name: Ahab
key_figures.description: King of Israel who promotes Baal worship and opposes Elijah.

key_figures.name: Jezebel
key_figures.description: Ahab's Phoenician wife, who persecutes the LORD's prophets and arranges Naboth's murder.

key_figures.name: Elijah
key_figures.description: The prophet who confronts Ahab, defeats the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and hears God's quiet voice at Horeb.

books.interpretive_notes: 1 and 2 Kings were originally a single book. Their chronology of the divided kingdom involves overlapping reigns and coregencies, so dates given by scholars can vary by several years.

books.name: 2 Kings
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; likely compiled from royal, prophetic, and historical sources.
books.original_audience: Judah and Israel, especially communities seeking to understand why both kingdoms fell.
books.purpose: To trace the decline and exile of Israel and Judah as the result of persistent covenant rebellion, while preserving signs of God's prophetic faithfulness.
books.historical_context: The book spans from Elijah's final days through the Assyrian destruction of the northern kingdom and Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem.
books.overall_theme: Persistent idolatry and injustice bring covenant judgment, yet God's word continues to prove reliable.
books.plain_english_summary: 2 Kings records prophetic ministries, royal reforms, repeated rebellion, the fall of Samaria, and finally the fall of Jerusalem and exile to Babylon.

major_events_or_movements.title: Elijah's Departure and Elisha's Ministry
major_events_or_movements.description: Elijah is taken up, and Elisha carries on a powerful prophetic ministry.

major_events_or_movements.title: Fall of the Northern Kingdom
major_events_or_movements.description: After generations of idolatry, Assyria captures Samaria and exiles Israel.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judah's Last Kings and Exile
major_events_or_movements.description: Despite reforms under Hezekiah and Josiah, Judah eventually falls to Babylon and Jerusalem is destroyed.

key_figures.name: Elijah
key_figures.description: Taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, passing his ministry to Elisha.

key_figures.name: Elisha
key_figures.description: Elijah's successor, whose ministry is marked by many miracles.

key_figures.name: Naaman
key_figures.description: An Aramean army commander healed of a skin disease after washing in the Jordan.

key_figures.name: Jehu
key_figures.description: Anointed king of Israel, who destroys Ahab's dynasty and Baal worship.

key_figures.name: Hezekiah
key_figures.description: A reforming king of Judah who trusts God when Assyria besieges Jerusalem.

key_figures.name: Isaiah
key_figures.description: The prophet who counsels Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis and his illness.

key_figures.name: Sennacherib
key_figures.description: King of Assyria, whose army threatens Jerusalem but is struck down.

key_figures.name: Manasseh
key_figures.description: Hezekiah's son, whose long and idolatrous reign is blamed for Judah's coming judgment.

key_figures.name: Josiah
key_figures.description: A king who leads sweeping reforms after the Book of the Law is found in the temple.

key_figures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
key_figures.description: King of Babylon, who conquers Judah, destroys Jerusalem, and carries the people into exile.

books.interpretive_notes: Scholars often read 1-2 Kings as part of a larger history shaped by Deuteronomy's covenant theology; the book ends with Jehoiachin's release in Babylon, which many read as a quiet note of hope for David's line.

books.name: 1 Chronicles
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; traditionally associated with Ezra, though the book itself does not name an author.
books.original_audience: The post-exilic Jewish community.
books.purpose: To retell Israel's history with special emphasis on David, temple worship, priesthood, and continuity with God's covenant promises.
books.historical_context: Written from a post-exilic perspective, Chronicles speaks to a restored but small community centered on Jerusalem and the temple.
books.overall_theme: God's people find identity and hope through covenant continuity, faithful worship, and the Davidic promise.
books.plain_english_summary: After extensive genealogies, 1 Chronicles focuses on David's reign, especially his preparation for the temple and organization of worship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Genealogies and Israel's Identity
major_events_or_movements.description: Long genealogies connect the post-exilic community with Israel's ancestral story.

major_events_or_movements.title: David's Reign
major_events_or_movements.description: David unites Israel, brings the ark to Jerusalem, and receives covenant promises.

major_events_or_movements.title: Preparation for the Temple
major_events_or_movements.description: David gathers materials and organizes Levites, priests, musicians, and leaders for future temple worship.

key_figures.name: David
key_figures.description: The central figure, presented as Israel's model king who organizes worship and prepares for the temple.

key_figures.name: Saul
key_figures.description: Israel's first king, whose death in battle opens the way for David's reign.

key_figures.name: Solomon
key_figures.description: David's son, chosen by God to build the temple.

key_figures.name: Nathan
key_figures.description: The prophet who delivers God's covenant promise to David.

key_figures.name: Jabez
key_figures.description: A man named in the genealogies who prays for God's blessing and protection.

key_figures.name: Asaph
key_figures.description: A Levite appointed by David to lead music and praise before the ark.

key_figures.name: Ornan the Jebusite
key_figures.description: Owner of the threshing floor that David purchases, which becomes the site of the temple.

books.interpretive_notes: Chronicles retells material from Samuel and Kings with its own emphases, often omitting David's failures and highlighting worship; readers generally see these choices as purposeful theology for the post-exilic community rather than contradiction.

books.name: 2 Chronicles
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; traditionally associated with Ezra.
books.original_audience: The post-exilic Jewish community.
books.purpose: To retell the history of Judah with emphasis on temple worship, reform, repentance, and the consequences of covenant faithfulness or rebellion.
books.historical_context: The book looks back on Solomon and the kings of Judah from the perspective of a community restored after Babylonian exile.
books.overall_theme: Seeking God brings renewal, while persistent unfaithfulness brings judgment; restoration remains possible through repentance.
books.plain_english_summary: 2 Chronicles begins with Solomon's temple, follows Judah's kings with special attention to reforms, and ends with exile and Cyrus's decree permitting return.

major_events_or_movements.title: Solomon Builds the Temple
major_events_or_movements.description: The temple is constructed, dedicated, and filled with God's glory.

major_events_or_movements.title: Reform and Apostasy among Judah's Kings
major_events_or_movements.description: Kings such as Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah pursue reforms, while others lead Judah into sin.

major_events_or_movements.title: Exile and Cyrus's Decree
major_events_or_movements.description: Jerusalem falls to Babylon, but the book ends with permission for the exiles to return and rebuild.

key_figures.name: Solomon
key_figures.description: Builds and dedicates the temple, which God's glory fills.

key_figures.name: The Queen of Sheba
key_figures.description: Visits Solomon and marvels at his wisdom.

key_figures.name: Rehoboam
key_figures.description: Solomon's son, during whose reign the kingdom divides.

key_figures.name: Asa
key_figures.description: A king of Judah who leads early reforms but later relies on foreign alliances.

key_figures.name: Jehoshaphat
key_figures.description: A king who sends teachers of the law and trusts God in battle.

key_figures.name: Joash
key_figures.description: Crowned as a child after Athaliah's usurpation; restores the temple but later turns away.

key_figures.name: Uzziah
key_figures.description: A strong king struck with a skin disease after pridefully burning incense in the temple.

key_figures.name: Hezekiah
key_figures.description: A king who reopens the temple, celebrates Passover, and trusts God against Assyria.

key_figures.name: Manasseh
key_figures.description: An idolatrous king who, uniquely in Chronicles, repents while in captivity.

key_figures.name: Josiah
key_figures.description: The last great reforming king, who renews the covenant and celebrates a great Passover.

key_figures.name: Cyrus
key_figures.description: King of Persia whose decree permits the exiles to return.

books.interpretive_notes: In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles is often the final book, so the canon closes with Cyrus' invitation to return and rebuild. Chronicles also uniquely records Manasseh's repentance (2 Chronicles 33).

books.name: Ezra
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Ezra; likely uses memoirs, lists, letters, and other records.
books.original_audience: The returned Jewish community in Judah.
books.purpose: To recount the return from exile, rebuilding of the temple, and Ezra's efforts to restore covenant faithfulness.
books.historical_context: The book is set under Persian rule after Cyrus allows exiled peoples to return and rebuild local religious institutions.
books.overall_theme: God restores His people, and restoration includes both rebuilt worship and renewed obedience.
books.plain_english_summary: Ezra recounts two major returns from exile: one connected with Zerubbabel and the temple, and a later one led by Ezra to address covenant faithfulness.

major_events_or_movements.title: Return and Altar Rebuilt
major_events_or_movements.description: A group returns under Persian authorization and restores sacrificial worship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Temple Rebuilt
major_events_or_movements.description: After opposition and delay, the second temple is completed.

major_events_or_movements.title: Ezra's Reform
major_events_or_movements.description: Ezra arrives with another group and addresses serious covenant concerns within the community.

key_figures.name: Cyrus
key_figures.description: King of Persia who issues the decree allowing the exiles to return and rebuild the temple.

key_figures.name: Zerubbabel
key_figures.description: A descendant of David who leads the first return and the rebuilding of the temple.

key_figures.name: Jeshua
key_figures.description: The high priest who works with Zerubbabel to restore the altar and temple.

key_figures.name: Haggai and Zechariah
key_figures.description: Prophets who encourage the people to resume temple construction.

key_figures.name: Darius
key_figures.description: Persian king who confirms Cyrus' decree and supports the completion of the temple.

key_figures.name: Artaxerxes
key_figures.description: Persian king who commissions Ezra to lead a later group and teach the law.

key_figures.name: Ezra
key_figures.description: A priest and scribe skilled in the law of Moses, who leads reforms in Jerusalem.

books.interpretive_notes: The intermarriage crisis in Ezra 9-10 is interpreted in light of covenant identity and idolatry concerns; readers should avoid treating it as a blanket ethnic principle.

books.name: Nehemiah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Largely based on Nehemiah's memoirs, with editorial shaping in its final form.
books.original_audience: The Jewish community in Jerusalem after exile.
books.purpose: To recount the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and the community's renewed commitment to covenant life.
books.historical_context: Nehemiah serves in the Persian court before becoming governor of Judah. Jerusalem remains vulnerable despite the rebuilt temple.
books.overall_theme: God's work includes both rebuilding a city and reforming a covenant community.
books.plain_english_summary: Nehemiah leads a rapid rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls despite opposition, then joins Ezra in public Scripture reading and covenant renewal before addressing ongoing social and religious problems.

major_events_or_movements.title: Walls Rebuilt
major_events_or_movements.description: Nehemiah organizes the people to rebuild Jerusalem's walls despite threats and opposition.

major_events_or_movements.title: Scripture Read and Covenant Renewed
major_events_or_movements.description: Ezra reads the law publicly, leading to confession, worship, and covenant commitment.

major_events_or_movements.title: Community Reforms
major_events_or_movements.description: Nehemiah addresses Sabbath observance, temple support, exploitation, and intermarriage concerns.

key_figures.name: Nehemiah
key_figures.description: Cupbearer to the Persian king, who becomes governor and leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.

key_figures.name: Artaxerxes
key_figures.description: The Persian king who grants Nehemiah permission and resources to rebuild.

key_figures.name: Ezra
key_figures.description: The priest and scribe who reads the law publicly to the people.

key_figures.name: Sanballat
key_figures.description: A regional official who leads opposition to the rebuilding.

key_figures.name: Tobiah
key_figures.description: An Ammonite official who opposes Nehemiah and is later expelled from a temple storeroom.

key_figures.name: Geshem the Arab
key_figures.description: Joins Sanballat and Tobiah in mocking and opposing the work.

key_figures.name: Eliashib
key_figures.description: The high priest, who helps rebuild the wall but later gives Tobiah a room in the temple.

books.interpretive_notes: Ezra and Nehemiah were treated as one book in ancient Jewish tradition. The relative order of Ezra's and Nehemiah's arrivals in Jerusalem is debated by some scholars.

books.name: Esther
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous.
books.original_audience: Jews living in the Persian Empire and later Jewish communities commemorating Purim.
books.purpose: To explain the deliverance of the Jewish people from a planned massacre and the origin of the feast of Purim.
books.historical_context: The story is set in the Persian Empire under King Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I, during the fifth century BC.
books.overall_theme: Providence can preserve God's people even when God is not explicitly named.
books.plain_english_summary: Esther, a Jewish woman who becomes queen, risks her life to expose Haman's plot against the Jews. The threatened destruction is reversed, and Purim commemorates the deliverance.

major_events_or_movements.title: Esther Becomes Queen
major_events_or_movements.description: Esther becomes queen of Persia while concealing her Jewish identity.

major_events_or_movements.title: Haman's Plot
major_events_or_movements.description: Haman gains authority and secures a decree to destroy the Jews after conflict with Mordecai.

major_events_or_movements.title: Reversal and Deliverance
major_events_or_movements.description: Esther exposes Haman, the Jews are allowed to defend themselves, and Purim is established.

key_figures.name: Esther
key_figures.description: A Jewish orphan, also named Hadassah, who becomes queen and risks her life to save her people.

key_figures.name: Mordecai
key_figures.description: Esther's cousin and guardian, whose refusal to bow to Haman triggers the conflict.

key_figures.name: Ahasuerus
key_figures.description: The Persian king, commonly identified with Xerxes I, who chooses Esther as queen.

key_figures.name: Haman
key_figures.description: An Agagite official who plots to destroy the Jews and is executed on his own gallows.

key_figures.name: Vashti
key_figures.description: The queen deposed for refusing the king's summons, opening the way for Esther.

books.interpretive_notes: The book never explicitly names God, leading many readers to emphasize divine providence while acknowledging that this is an inference from the narrative.

books.name: Job
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; the historical setting of Job and the date of composition are uncertain.
books.original_audience: Wisdom readers wrestling with suffering, justice, and the limits of human understanding.
books.purpose: To explore why righteous people suffer and to challenge simplistic explanations that equate suffering directly with personal sin.
books.historical_context: Job is set in the land of Uz rather than Israel, giving the book a broad human focus. Its language and composition are difficult to date with certainty.
books.overall_theme: Human beings do not possess God's full perspective; faithful trust is necessary when suffering cannot be neatly explained.
books.plain_english_summary: Job loses family, wealth, and health. His friends insist suffering must prove guilt, but God ultimately exposes the limits of their explanations and confronts Job with the vastness of divine wisdom.

major_events_or_movements.title: Job's Catastrophic Losses
major_events_or_movements.description: Job loses possessions, children, and health yet continues wrestling with faith.

major_events_or_movements.title: Debates with Friends
major_events_or_movements.description: Job and his three friends argue over suffering, justice, innocence, and God's ways; a younger speaker, Elihu, then adds his own response.

major_events_or_movements.title: God Answers and Job Responds
major_events_or_movements.description: God speaks from the whirlwind, emphasizing divine wisdom and human limitation; Job responds in humility.

key_figures.name: Job
key_figures.description: A blameless man from Uz who loses everything and wrestles with God over his suffering.

key_figures.name: The Accuser (Satan)
key_figures.description: A heavenly figure who questions Job's integrity and is permitted to test him.

key_figures.name: Job's wife
key_figures.description: Urges Job, in his despair, to curse God and die.

key_figures.name: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar
key_figures.description: Job's three friends, who insist his suffering must result from sin and are later rebuked by God.

key_figures.name: Elihu
key_figures.description: A younger speaker who responds to both Job and his friends before God speaks.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpreters differ on whether Job is historical narrative, a didactic story, or both; most agree that God's speeches do not explain Job's suffering but reorient him to God's wisdom and power.

books.name: Psalms
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: A collection by multiple authors, prominently David, but also Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, and anonymous writers.
books.original_audience: Israel's worshiping community, later used widely in Jewish and Christian prayer and worship.
books.purpose: To provide songs and prayers for worship, lament, thanksgiving, wisdom, kingship, confession, and hope.
books.historical_context: The Psalter developed over time and reflects many periods of Israel's history, including monarchy, crisis, exile, and restoration.
books.overall_theme: Every part of human life can be brought honestly before God in worship and trust.
books.plain_english_summary: Psalms is a five-book collection of 150 prayers and songs ranging from deep grief to exuberant praise. It teaches God's people to pray honestly while grounding hope in God's character and kingship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Lament and Trust
major_events_or_movements.description: Many psalms bring fear, injustice, guilt, and grief before God while moving toward trust.

major_events_or_movements.title: Kingship and Messianic Hope
major_events_or_movements.description: Royal psalms celebrate God's rule and the Davidic king, later read by Christians in relation to Christ.

major_events_or_movements.title: Praise and Thanksgiving
major_events_or_movements.description: The collection repeatedly calls individuals and communities to praise God for creation, rescue, and covenant faithfulness.

key_figures.name: David
key_figures.description: The psalmist most often named in the superscriptions, associated with seventy-three psalms in the Hebrew text.

key_figures.name: Asaph
key_figures.description: A Levitical worship leader linked with twelve psalms (Psalm 50 and 73-83).

key_figures.name: The Sons of Korah
key_figures.description: A Levitical guild of singers associated with eleven psalms, including Psalms 42 and 84.

key_figures.name: Solomon
key_figures.description: Named in the superscriptions of Psalms 72 and 127.

key_figures.name: Moses
key_figures.description: Named as the author of Psalm 90, traditionally the oldest psalm in the collection.

key_figures.name: Heman and Ethan
key_figures.description: Ezrahite sages credited with Psalms 88 and 89.

books.interpretive_notes: Some psalms are interpreted messianically in the New Testament; Christian traditions may differ on how directly particular texts predict Christ.

books.name: Proverbs
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: A wisdom collection associated especially with Solomon, with material also linked to other sages such as Agur and Lemuel.
books.original_audience: Israel and anyone seeking practical wisdom for faithful living.
books.purpose: To train readers in skillful, God-centered living across speech, work, money, relationships, sexuality, justice, and self-control.
books.historical_context: Proverbs reflects the wisdom tradition of the ancient Near East while grounding wisdom in reverence for the LORD.
books.overall_theme: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and wise living normally produces patterns of life aligned with God's order.
books.plain_english_summary: Proverbs combines extended teaching with short sayings that contrast wisdom and folly. Its sayings are general principles, not unconditional guarantees about every circumstance.

major_events_or_movements.title: Call to Wisdom
major_events_or_movements.description: Early chapters personify wisdom and warn against destructive choices.

major_events_or_movements.title: Solomonic Proverbs
major_events_or_movements.description: Short sayings address everyday conduct, speech, diligence, justice, and relationships.

major_events_or_movements.title: Final Collections
major_events_or_movements.description: Sayings of Agur and Lemuel conclude the book, including the portrait of the capable woman.

key_figures.name: Solomon
key_figures.description: King of Israel credited with the main collections of proverbs.

key_figures.name: Hezekiah's men
key_figures.description: Scribes in King Hezekiah's court who copied a further collection of Solomon's proverbs (chapters 25-29).

key_figures.name: Agur son of Jakeh
key_figures.description: A sage whose humble and numerical sayings appear in chapter 30.

key_figures.name: King Lemuel and his mother
key_figures.description: Lemuel records his mother's counsel on just rule and the portrait of the capable woman (chapter 31).

key_figures.name: Lady Wisdom and Woman Folly
key_figures.description: Personified figures in chapters 1-9 who call out to the simple, inviting them to life or to death.

books.interpretive_notes: Proverbs should usually be read as wise generalizations rather than promises that remove all exceptions.

books.name: Ecclesiastes
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Attributed to 'Qoheleth' or 'the Teacher,' traditionally identified with Solomon; many scholars debate that identification.
books.original_audience: Readers confronting life's brevity, frustration, and apparent unpredictability.
books.purpose: To expose the limits of life pursued 'under the sun' and to direct readers toward humble enjoyment of God's gifts and reverence for God.
books.historical_context: The book belongs to Israel's wisdom tradition and reflects on work, wealth, pleasure, injustice, aging, and death.
books.overall_theme: Life is fleeting and often puzzling; receive God's gifts gratefully, live wisely, and fear God.
books.plain_english_summary: Ecclesiastes tests pleasure, achievement, wealth, and wisdom and finds that none can defeat death or guarantee lasting control. It counsels realistic joy and reverence before God.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Teacher's Search
major_events_or_movements.description: The Teacher examines wisdom, pleasure, work, and achievement and finds them unable to provide ultimate permanence.

major_events_or_movements.title: Reflections on Time and Injustice
major_events_or_movements.description: The book considers seasons of life, oppression, wealth, and the unpredictability of outcomes.

major_events_or_movements.title: Final Counsel
major_events_or_movements.description: Readers are urged to enjoy life responsibly, remember their Creator, and fear God.

key_figures.name: Qoheleth (the Teacher)
key_figures.description: The main speaker, described as a son of David and king in Jerusalem, who searches for meaning 'under the sun.'

key_figures.name: The frame narrator
key_figures.description: The voice that introduces the Teacher and closes the book with the call to fear God and keep His commandments.

books.interpretive_notes: The Hebrew word often translated 'vanity' can carry the sense of vapor, breath, or elusiveness; interpretations vary on whether the tone is primarily pessimistic, realistic, or pedagogical.

books.name: Song of Solomon
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with Solomon; the collection may include multiple poetic voices.
books.original_audience: Israel and later Jewish and Christian readers reflecting on love, desire, and marriage.
books.purpose: To celebrate romantic love, mutual desire, beauty, and committed affection.
books.historical_context: The book is love poetry from the ancient Near East and contains dialogue among lovers and companions.
books.overall_theme: Human romantic love is powerful, beautiful, and worthy of honor when expressed with mutuality and commitment.
books.plain_english_summary: Song of Solomon is a collection of poems celebrating attraction, longing, delight, separation, reunion, and the strength of love.

major_events_or_movements.title: Courtship and Desire
major_events_or_movements.description: The lovers praise one another and express longing for closeness.

major_events_or_movements.title: Separation and Search
major_events_or_movements.description: Several poems portray absence, searching, and renewed encounter.

major_events_or_movements.title: Love's Strength Celebrated
major_events_or_movements.description: The book culminates in a declaration that love is powerful and cannot simply be bought.

key_figures.name: The woman (the Shulammite)
key_figures.description: The beloved woman, the main voice of the poems, who expresses longing and delight.

key_figures.name: The man (the beloved)
key_figures.description: Her lover, who praises her beauty and returns her affection.

key_figures.name: Solomon
key_figures.description: Named in the title and in scenes such as the royal procession; interpreters differ on whether he is the lover or a contrasting figure.

key_figures.name: The daughters of Jerusalem
key_figures.description: A chorus of women whom the woman addresses, including the repeated charge not to awaken love before its time.

books.interpretive_notes: Jewish and Christian traditions have often read the book allegorically as depicting God's love for His people, while many modern interpreters emphasize its primary sense as human love poetry.

books.name: Isaiah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Isaiah son of Amoz is the named prophet; many scholars debate how the book reached its final form and whether later sections involve additional prophetic voices or disciples.
books.original_audience: Judah and Jerusalem across periods of Assyrian threat, judgment, exile-related hope, and anticipated restoration.
books.purpose: To confront Judah's sin, announce judgment, reveal God's holiness and sovereignty, and proclaim future restoration and hope.
books.historical_context: Isaiah's ministry begins in the eighth century BC amid Assyrian expansion. Later portions address exile and restoration themes that extend beyond Isaiah's immediate historical setting.
books.overall_theme: The Holy One of Israel judges sin yet promises salvation, restoration, and a future righteous ruler and servant.
books.plain_english_summary: Isaiah moves between severe warnings and sweeping hope. It confronts idolatry and injustice, promises a coming king and servant, and looks toward renewed creation and restored Zion.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judgment, Isaiah's Call, and the Assyrian Crisis
major_events_or_movements.description: Isaiah indicts Judah's sin, encounters God's holiness in his call vision, and ministers during Judah's conflict with Assyria.

major_events_or_movements.title: Comfort and Return
major_events_or_movements.description: The book announces comfort, God's incomparable rule, and hope for return from exile.

major_events_or_movements.title: Servant, Restoration, and New Creation
major_events_or_movements.description: Servant songs, salvation promises, and visions of renewed Zion and creation dominate the closing sections.

key_figures.name: Isaiah
key_figures.description: The prophet son of Amoz, who sees the LORD enthroned and ministers in Jerusalem for decades.

key_figures.name: Uzziah
key_figures.description: King of Judah in the year of whose death Isaiah receives his call vision.

key_figures.name: Ahaz
key_figures.description: King of Judah who refuses to trust God during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis and is given the Immanuel sign.

key_figures.name: Hezekiah
key_figures.description: King of Judah who seeks the LORD when Assyria besieges Jerusalem.

key_figures.name: Sennacherib
key_figures.description: King of Assyria whose army threatens Jerusalem and is struck down.

key_figures.name: Cyrus
key_figures.description: The Persian king named as the LORD's anointed instrument to free the exiles.

key_figures.name: The Servant of the LORD
key_figures.description: The figure of the Servant Songs who brings justice and suffers for others; the New Testament identifies him with Jesus.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians broadly read many passages christologically, though traditions and scholars differ on the immediate and ultimate referents of specific prophecies.

books.name: Jeremiah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, with assistance from the scribe Baruch in preserving and transmitting his messages.
books.original_audience: Judah and Jerusalem in the final decades before and during Babylonian conquest.
books.purpose: To warn Judah of coming judgment for covenant rebellion, call for repentance, and promise eventual restoration and a new covenant.
books.historical_context: Jeremiah ministers from the reign of Josiah through Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC, amid political instability between Egypt and Babylon.
books.overall_theme: Persistent rebellion brings judgment, yet God promises restoration and a new covenant written on the heart.
books.plain_english_summary: Jeremiah spends decades warning Judah that Babylonian conquest is coming. He suffers rejection, witnesses Jerusalem's fall, and still proclaims hope for restoration and a new covenant.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jeremiah's Call and Warnings
major_events_or_movements.description: Jeremiah is appointed as a prophet and repeatedly warns Judah to turn from idolatry and injustice.

major_events_or_movements.title: Conflict and Persecution
major_events_or_movements.description: Jeremiah faces priests, prophets, kings, imprisonment, and public hostility over his message.

major_events_or_movements.title: Fall of Jerusalem and New Covenant Hope
major_events_or_movements.description: Jeremiah announces restoration and a new covenant, Jerusalem falls to Babylon, and the book closes with oracles against the nations and an account of the city's fall.

key_figures.name: Jeremiah
key_figures.description: The 'weeping prophet,' called as a youth to warn Judah of coming judgment.

key_figures.name: Baruch
key_figures.description: Jeremiah's scribe and companion, who records and reads his messages.

key_figures.name: Josiah
key_figures.description: The reforming king during whose reign Jeremiah's ministry begins.

key_figures.name: Jehoiakim
key_figures.description: King of Judah who burns Jeremiah's scroll in defiance.

key_figures.name: Zedekiah
key_figures.description: Judah's last king, who consults Jeremiah secretly but refuses to obey.

key_figures.name: Hananiah
key_figures.description: A false prophet who contradicts Jeremiah and dies within the year as Jeremiah foretold.

key_figures.name: Ebed-melech
key_figures.description: A Cushite official who rescues Jeremiah from a muddy cistern.

key_figures.name: Gedaliah
key_figures.description: Governor appointed by Babylon after Jerusalem's fall, who is assassinated.

key_figures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
key_figures.description: King of Babylon, whom Jeremiah calls God's servant in bringing judgment on Judah.

books.interpretive_notes: The Greek Septuagint version of Jeremiah is shorter than the Hebrew text and arranges some material differently, reflecting a complex process of preservation; Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah 31's new covenant promise as fulfilled in Christ.

books.name: Lamentations
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book itself does not name him.
books.original_audience: The devastated community of Judah after Jerusalem's fall.
books.purpose: To give poetic voice to grief over Jerusalem's destruction while preserving confession, prayer, and hope in God's mercy.
books.historical_context: The poems reflect the aftermath of Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
books.overall_theme: Faith can lament honestly in catastrophe while still appealing to God's compassion and faithfulness.
books.plain_english_summary: Lamentations is a collection of five poems grieving Jerusalem's destruction. It refuses easy answers, acknowledges sin and judgment, and still looks to God's mercies as a basis for hope.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jerusalem Mourned
major_events_or_movements.description: The city is personified as a grieving widow after destruction and exile.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judgment and Deep Suffering
major_events_or_movements.description: The poems describe siege, hunger, violence, and the experience of divine judgment.

major_events_or_movements.title: Hope in the Middle of Grief
major_events_or_movements.description: The central poem recalls God's steadfast mercy even while suffering continues.

key_figures.name: Jeremiah (traditional author)
key_figures.description: Long associated with the book, though the poems themselves do not name their author.

key_figures.name: Daughter Zion
key_figures.description: Jerusalem personified as a grieving widow who mourns her children and her ruin.

key_figures.name: The man who has seen affliction
key_figures.description: The individual voice of chapter 3, who moves from deep suffering to hope in God's mercies.

books.interpretive_notes: Chapters 1-4 are acrostic poems that follow the Hebrew alphabet, giving structure to grief; Lamentations is read in Jewish tradition on Tisha B'Av, which commemorates the temple's destruction.

books.name: Ezekiel
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Ezekiel, a priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon.
books.original_audience: Judean exiles in Babylon before and after Jerusalem's destruction.
books.purpose: To explain judgment on Jerusalem, defend God's justice, call for repentance, and proclaim future restoration and renewed divine presence.
books.historical_context: Ezekiel was exiled to Babylon in 597 BC and ministered there as Jerusalem moved toward destruction in 586 BC.
books.overall_theme: God's glory is not confined to Jerusalem; He judges rebellion, gives new life, and promises restored presence among His people.
books.plain_english_summary: Ezekiel receives dramatic visions and symbolic acts announcing Jerusalem's fall. After the city is destroyed, his message turns strongly toward restoration, new hearts, revived people, and a renewed temple vision.

major_events_or_movements.title: Vision and Call
major_events_or_movements.description: Ezekiel sees God's mobile throne and is commissioned as a watchman to the exiles.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jerusalem's Judgment
major_events_or_movements.description: Symbolic actions and visions announce the city's corruption and coming destruction.

major_events_or_movements.title: Restoration Visions
major_events_or_movements.description: The valley of dry bones, reunited people, and temple vision depict future renewal and God's returning presence.

key_figures.name: Ezekiel
key_figures.description: A priest exiled to Babylon, called as a prophet and watchman through dramatic visions.

key_figures.name: Jehoiachin
key_figures.description: The exiled king of Judah, from whose deportation Ezekiel dates his prophecies.

key_figures.name: The elders of Israel
key_figures.description: Exiled leaders who come to Ezekiel for counsel and are confronted about their idolatry.

key_figures.name: Ezekiel's wife
key_figures.description: Her sudden death becomes a sign of the coming loss of the temple.

key_figures.name: The shepherd prince
key_figures.description: A future ruler from David's line whom God promises to set over His restored people.

key_figures.name: Gog of Magog
key_figures.description: A symbolic enemy leader whose final assault against God's people is defeated.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpretations vary widely regarding the fulfillment and symbolism of Ezekiel 40-48, especially the temple vision.

books.name: Daniel
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: The book centers on Daniel, a Judean exile; Jewish and Christian traditions differ with some modern scholars over the date and composition of the final book.
books.original_audience: Jews living under foreign empires and facing pressure to compromise.
books.purpose: To encourage faithful endurance by showing God's sovereignty over kings, empires, persecution, and history.
books.historical_context: The narratives are set in Babylonian and Persian courts; the visions portray successive kingdoms and periods of severe oppression.
books.overall_theme: God rules over human empires and will ultimately establish His kingdom, so His people can remain faithful under pressure.
books.plain_english_summary: Daniel combines court stories of faithful Jews in exile with symbolic visions about kingdoms, persecution, judgment, and God's final rule.

major_events_or_movements.title: Faithfulness in Babylon
major_events_or_movements.description: Daniel and his friends resist assimilation pressures while serving in foreign courts.

major_events_or_movements.title: Fiery Furnace and Lions' Den
major_events_or_movements.description: Daniel's friends and Daniel himself face death for refusing to compromise worship and prayer.

major_events_or_movements.title: Apocalyptic Visions
major_events_or_movements.description: Daniel sees symbolic visions of beasts, kingdoms, heavenly judgment, and future deliverance.

key_figures.name: Daniel
key_figures.description: A Judean exile, renamed Belteshazzar, who stays faithful in the Babylonian and Persian courts and receives visions.

key_figures.name: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego
key_figures.description: Daniel's companions (Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah), who refuse to worship the king's image and are delivered from the furnace.

key_figures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
key_figures.description: King of Babylon, humbled by God until he acknowledges the Most High.

key_figures.name: Belshazzar
key_figures.description: Babylonian ruler who sees the writing on the wall the night his kingdom falls.

key_figures.name: Darius the Mede
key_figures.description: The ruler under whom Daniel is thrown into the lions' den.

key_figures.name: Gabriel and Michael
key_figures.description: Angels who appear in the visions: Gabriel interprets them, and Michael is described as a prince who protects Daniel's people.

key_figures.name: One like a son of man
key_figures.description: A heavenly figure who receives everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days; Jesus applies this title to Himself.

books.interpretive_notes: Christian traditions differ significantly in how they identify the kingdoms and future fulfillments in Daniel's apocalyptic visions.

books.name: Hosea
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Hosea son of Beeri.
books.original_audience: The northern kingdom of Israel, with implications for Judah.
books.purpose: To expose Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and proclaim God's persistent love, judgment, and desire for restoration.
books.historical_context: Hosea ministers in the eighth century BC as the northern kingdom approaches Assyrian conquest in 722 BC.
books.overall_theme: Israel's spiritual adultery brings judgment, yet God's covenant love continues to call His people back.
books.plain_english_summary: Hosea's troubled marriage becomes a living sign of Israel's unfaithfulness. The prophet condemns idolatry and injustice while repeatedly expressing God's grief, love, and hope for return.

major_events_or_movements.title: Hosea's Marriage as a Sign
major_events_or_movements.description: Hosea's family life symbolizes Israel's unfaithfulness and the painful covenant relationship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Charges against Israel
major_events_or_movements.description: The prophet condemns idolatry, political alliances, corruption, and lack of true knowledge of God.

major_events_or_movements.title: Love and Restoration
major_events_or_movements.description: God's parental and covenant love remains visible even in judgment, ending with a call to return.

key_figures.name: Hosea
key_figures.description: Prophet to the northern kingdom whose marriage becomes a sign of Israel's unfaithfulness.

key_figures.name: Gomer
key_figures.description: Hosea's wife, whose unfaithfulness mirrors Israel's spiritual adultery.

key_figures.name: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, and Lo-ammi
key_figures.description: Hosea's children, whose names announce judgment and are later reversed in promises of restoration.

key_figures.name: Jeroboam II
key_figures.description: King of Israel during Hosea's ministry.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpreters debate whether Gomer was unfaithful before or after marrying Hosea and whether the marriage narrative is literal or partly symbolic; the theological point of God's faithful love is clear either way.

books.name: Joel
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Joel son of Pethuel.
books.original_audience: Judah and Jerusalem.
books.purpose: To interpret a devastating locust plague as a call to repentance and to point toward the coming day of the LORD, restoration, and outpouring of God's Spirit.
books.historical_context: The exact date is debated because Joel names no king. The book describes agricultural devastation, communal crisis, and temple-centered worship.
books.overall_theme: Present crisis calls for wholehearted repentance, while the day of the LORD brings both judgment and salvation.
books.plain_english_summary: Joel begins with a locust disaster and summons the whole community to repentance. It then expands to the day of the LORD, promising restoration and the outpouring of God's Spirit.

major_events_or_movements.title: Locust Plague
major_events_or_movements.description: A devastating swarm destroys crops and disrupts normal worship and economy.

major_events_or_movements.title: Call to Repentance
major_events_or_movements.description: Priests and people are summoned to fast, gather, and return to God with their whole hearts.

major_events_or_movements.title: Restoration and Spirit
major_events_or_movements.description: God promises renewed abundance, the outpouring of the Spirit, and final judgment among the nations.

key_figures.name: Joel
key_figures.description: The prophet son of Pethuel, who calls Judah to repentance after a locust plague.

key_figures.name: The priests
key_figures.description: The 'ministers of the altar,' summoned to lead the people in fasting and prayer.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians connect Joel 2:28-32 with Pentecost through Acts 2, while differing on how the remaining day-of-the-LORD imagery relates to future events.

books.name: Amos
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Amos, a shepherd and cultivator from Tekoa in Judah.
books.original_audience: Primarily the northern kingdom of Israel.
books.purpose: To announce judgment on Israel for injustice, exploitation, false worship, and complacency while affirming God's moral rule over all nations.
books.historical_context: Amos prophesies in the eighth century BC during a period of prosperity under Jeroboam II, shortly before Assyrian pressure intensifies.
books.overall_theme: Religious activity without justice and covenant faithfulness is unacceptable to God.
books.plain_english_summary: Amos confronts a prosperous society in which the wealthy exploit the vulnerable while maintaining impressive religious observance. He announces coming judgment and ends with a promise of restoration.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judgments on the Nations
major_events_or_movements.description: Amos begins by announcing God's judgment on neighboring nations and then turns sharply toward Israel.

major_events_or_movements.title: Condemnation of Injustice and Empty Worship
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel's luxury, oppression, and religious hypocrisy are exposed.

major_events_or_movements.title: Visions of Judgment and Restoration
major_events_or_movements.description: A series of visions culminates in judgment, followed by a closing promise of restoration.

key_figures.name: Amos
key_figures.description: A shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah sent to prophesy against the northern kingdom.

key_figures.name: Amaziah
key_figures.description: The priest of Bethel who accuses Amos of conspiracy and orders him to leave.

key_figures.name: Jeroboam II
key_figures.description: King of Israel during a time of prosperity and injustice.

key_figures.name: Uzziah
key_figures.description: King of Judah during Amos' ministry.

books.interpretive_notes: Amos is frequently cited in discussions of social justice. The closing promise of restoration (Amos 9:11-12) is quoted by James at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.

books.name: Obadiah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Obadiah; little else is known about the prophet.
books.original_audience: Judah and surrounding peoples in the context of Edom's hostility.
books.purpose: To announce judgment on Edom for pride and violence against Judah and to affirm the LORD's ultimate rule.
books.historical_context: The book likely reflects a period when Jerusalem suffered attack and Edom took advantage of Judah's disaster; many connect it with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem.
books.overall_theme: Pride and violence against others invite judgment; the LORD's kingdom will ultimately prevail.
books.plain_english_summary: Obadiah is the shortest Old Testament book. It condemns Edom for gloating over Judah's fall and promises that unjust power will not have the final word.

major_events_or_movements.title: Edom's Pride Exposed
major_events_or_movements.description: Edom trusts in its mountain strongholds and political security.

major_events_or_movements.title: Violence against Judah Condemned
major_events_or_movements.description: Edom is accused of standing aloof, gloating, looting, and helping trap survivors during Jerusalem's disaster.

major_events_or_movements.title: Day of the LORD
major_events_or_movements.description: Edom's fate is placed within a wider vision of judgment and the LORD's kingdom.

key_figures.name: Obadiah
key_figures.description: The prophet, about whom almost nothing else is known.

key_figures.name: Edom (Esau)
key_figures.description: The nation descended from Esau, condemned for pride and violence against Judah.

key_figures.name: The house of Jacob
key_figures.description: God's people, promised deliverance and restored possession of their land.

books.interpretive_notes: The date of Obadiah is debated; most connect it with Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, while others suggest an earlier attack. Obadiah shares close parallels with Jeremiah 49.

books.name: Jonah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: The narrative centers on Jonah son of Amittai; the book itself is anonymous as a literary work.
books.original_audience: Israel and later readers wrestling with God's mercy toward outsiders.
books.purpose: To confront narrow nationalism and show God's compassion even toward a violent foreign city when people repent.
books.historical_context: Nineveh was a major Assyrian city. Assyria later became a brutal imperial power over Israel and its neighbors.
books.overall_theme: God's mercy extends beyond Israel, and His servants must learn to value the people He is willing to forgive.
books.plain_english_summary: Jonah flees from God's call to preach in Nineveh, is rescued through the great fish, reluctantly preaches, and becomes angry when the city repents and is spared.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jonah Flees
major_events_or_movements.description: Jonah runs from God's commission, leading to a storm and his being thrown into the sea.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jonah Rescued and Sent Again
major_events_or_movements.description: Jonah prays from the fish and then receives the commission a second time.

major_events_or_movements.title: Nineveh Repents and Jonah Resents Mercy
major_events_or_movements.description: The city responds to warning, God relents from announced disaster, and Jonah struggles with God's compassion.

key_figures.name: Jonah
key_figures.description: A prophet son of Amittai who flees God's call to Nineveh and later resents God's mercy.

key_figures.name: The sailors
key_figures.description: Pagan mariners who fear the LORD after the storm is calmed.

key_figures.name: The king of Nineveh
key_figures.description: Leads his city in fasting and repentance after Jonah's warning.

key_figures.name: The people of Nineveh
key_figures.description: The Assyrian city's inhabitants, who believe God and are spared.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians differ on questions about the genre and historical details of Jonah; the narrative's theological emphasis on repentance and mercy remains central.

books.name: Micah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Micah of Moresheth.
books.original_audience: Judah and Israel, especially Jerusalem and Samaria.
books.purpose: To denounce injustice, idolatry, corrupt leadership, and false security while promising restoration and a future ruler.
books.historical_context: Micah ministers in the eighth century BC during Assyrian expansion and overlaps the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in Judah.
books.overall_theme: God requires justice, faithful love, and humble walking with Him; judgment is real, but restoration is promised.
