books.plain_english_summary: Micah alternates between judgment and hope. He condemns abusive leaders and empty confidence in religious institutions while promising a future ruler from Bethlehem and renewed peace.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem
major_events_or_movements.description: Micah announces judgment on both capitals for idolatry and corruption.

major_events_or_movements.title: Future Peace and Ruler
major_events_or_movements.description: The prophet envisions restored Zion and a ruler from Bethlehem.

major_events_or_movements.title: Covenant Lawsuit and Hope
major_events_or_movements.description: God's case against His people culminates in the call to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly, followed by hope in divine forgiveness.

key_figures.name: Micah
key_figures.description: A prophet from the small town of Moresheth who confronts injustice in Jerusalem and Samaria.

key_figures.name: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah
key_figures.description: The kings of Judah during whose reigns Micah prophesies.

key_figures.name: Corrupt leaders, priests, and prophets
key_figures.description: Those Micah condemns for exploiting the people and teaching for money.

key_figures.name: The ruler from Bethlehem
key_figures.description: A promised shepherd-king whose origins are from of old; Matthew connects this with Jesus.

books.interpretive_notes: Matthew 2:6 cites Micah 5:2 in connection with Jesus' birth in Bethlehem. Micah 4:1-3 closely parallels Isaiah 2:2-4, and Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah directly.

books.name: Nahum
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Nahum of Elkosh.
books.original_audience: Judah, with Nineveh and Assyria as the subject of judgment.
books.purpose: To announce the fall of Nineveh and reassure Judah that Assyrian oppression would not last forever.
books.historical_context: Nahum speaks after Assyria's destruction of the northern kingdom and likely before Nineveh fell to Babylonian and Median forces in 612 BC.
books.overall_theme: God's justice will bring down violent empires, and oppressors do not rule forever.
books.plain_english_summary: Nahum is an oracle celebrating the coming collapse of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian Empire, whose brutality had devastated many nations.

major_events_or_movements.title: The LORD as Judge and Refuge
major_events_or_movements.description: An opening poem presents God as patient yet just, powerful yet a refuge for those who trust Him.

major_events_or_movements.title: Nineveh's Fall Described
major_events_or_movements.description: Vivid battle imagery portrays the city's coming defeat.

major_events_or_movements.title: Reasons for Judgment
major_events_or_movements.description: Nineveh's violence, exploitation, and arrogance are named as reasons for its downfall.

key_figures.name: Nahum
key_figures.description: The prophet from Elkosh who announces Nineveh's fall.

key_figures.name: The king of Assyria
key_figures.description: Addressed at the end of the book as his shepherds slumber and his people are scattered.

books.interpretive_notes: Nahum is sometimes read alongside Jonah: Jonah shows Nineveh spared after repentance, while Nahum announces its later downfall, together showing both God's mercy and His justice.

books.name: Habakkuk
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Habakkuk the prophet.
books.original_audience: Judah during the rise of Babylon.
books.purpose: To wrestle honestly with injustice and explain that God will use Babylon as judgment yet will also judge Babylon, calling the righteous to live by faithfulness.
books.historical_context: The book likely comes from the late seventh century BC as Babylon emerges as the dominant regional power.
books.overall_theme: Faith trusts God's justice and character even when His timing and methods are difficult to understand.
books.plain_english_summary: Habakkuk complains about violence in Judah, is shocked that God will use Babylon as judgment, and finally moves from questioning to worshipful trust.

major_events_or_movements.title: First Complaint: Judah's Violence
major_events_or_movements.description: Habakkuk asks why God seems to tolerate injustice among His people.

major_events_or_movements.title: Second Complaint and God's Answer
major_events_or_movements.description: Habakkuk questions Babylon's role, and God declares that proud empires will also face judgment.

major_events_or_movements.title: Prayer of Trust
major_events_or_movements.description: The prophet ends with a poetic prayer that rejoices in God even if crops and herds fail.

key_figures.name: Habakkuk
key_figures.description: A prophet who brings honest complaints to God and ends in trusting praise.

key_figures.name: The Chaldeans (Babylonians)
key_figures.description: The fierce nation God raises up to judge Judah, and who will themselves be judged.

books.interpretive_notes: Habakkuk 2:4, 'the righteous shall live by his faith,' is quoted in Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews and became central in Reformation discussions of justification.

books.name: Zephaniah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Zephaniah son of Cushi.
books.original_audience: Judah and Jerusalem during the reign of Josiah.
books.purpose: To warn of the coming day of the LORD, call for repentance, and promise purification and restoration for a humble remnant.
books.historical_context: Zephaniah ministers in the seventh century BC, likely before or around Josiah's reforms, amid idolatry and social corruption.
books.overall_theme: The day of the LORD exposes sin but also leads to purification, humility, and restored joy.
books.plain_english_summary: Zephaniah announces sweeping judgment on Judah and the nations, urges the humble to seek the LORD, and closes with a tender vision of God rejoicing over a restored people.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judgment on Judah
major_events_or_movements.description: Idolatry, complacency, and injustice in Jerusalem are condemned.

major_events_or_movements.title: Judgment on Nations
major_events_or_movements.description: Neighboring nations and major powers are included under God's judgment.

major_events_or_movements.title: Purified and Restored People
major_events_or_movements.description: The book ends with promises of humble worship, restored fortunes, and divine joy over His people.

key_figures.name: Zephaniah
key_figures.description: The prophet son of Cushi, whose genealogy traces back to a Hezekiah, possibly the king.

key_figures.name: Josiah
key_figures.description: King of Judah during whose reign Zephaniah prophesies.

key_figures.name: The humble remnant
key_figures.description: Those who seek the LORD and are promised refuge and restoration.

books.interpretive_notes: Zephaniah's 'day of the LORD' imagery shaped later Christian reflection on final judgment, including the medieval hymn Dies Irae; interpreters differ on how much refers to near events and how much to final judgment.

books.name: Haggai
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Haggai the prophet.
books.original_audience: The returned Jewish community in Judah, especially leaders Zerubbabel and Joshua.
books.purpose: To urge the post-exilic community to rebuild the temple and reorder priorities around covenant worship.
books.historical_context: Haggai speaks in 520 BC under Persian rule, after temple rebuilding had stalled for years.
books.overall_theme: God's people must put His priorities ahead of complacent self-interest; renewed obedience brings courage and hope.
books.plain_english_summary: Haggai delivers four dated messages challenging returned exiles to rebuild the temple. He connects economic frustration with misplaced priorities and promises God's presence with the work.

major_events_or_movements.title: Call to Rebuild
major_events_or_movements.description: Haggai confronts the people for living in finished houses while the temple remains in ruins.

major_events_or_movements.title: Encouragement amid Discouragement
major_events_or_movements.description: Those who remember the former temple are encouraged that God's presence remains with them.

major_events_or_movements.title: Promises of Cleansing and Future Hope
major_events_or_movements.description: Haggai links renewed obedience with blessing and gives Zerubbabel a sign of future covenant significance.

key_figures.name: Haggai
key_figures.description: A prophet who urges the returned exiles to rebuild the temple.

key_figures.name: Zerubbabel
key_figures.description: Governor of Judah and descendant of David, called God's 'signet ring.'

key_figures.name: Joshua son of Jehozadak
key_figures.description: The high priest, who leads the people in resuming the work.

key_figures.name: Darius
key_figures.description: The Persian king by whose reign Haggai's messages are dated.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpreters differ on whether the promise to 'shake the nations' and fill the temple with glory (Haggai 2:6-9) refers to the second temple's adornment, a messianic fulfillment, or both; Hebrews 12:26-27 applies the shaking language to final judgment.

books.name: Zechariah
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Zechariah son of Berechiah, with scholarly debate over the composition of chapters 9-14.
books.original_audience: The post-exilic community in Judah.
books.purpose: To encourage temple rebuilding, call for repentance, and expand hope toward future purification, kingship, and God's universal reign.
books.historical_context: Zechariah begins in 520 BC alongside Haggai during Persian rule and the rebuilding of the temple.
books.overall_theme: God has not abandoned His people; present restoration points toward a larger future work of cleansing, kingship, and worldwide rule.
books.plain_english_summary: Zechariah combines symbolic night visions with prophetic messages about rebuilding, priestly cleansing, a coming king, future conflict, and the LORD's final reign.

major_events_or_movements.title: Night Visions
major_events_or_movements.description: A series of symbolic visions reassures the community that God remembers Jerusalem and will deal with opposition and sin.

major_events_or_movements.title: Temple and True Obedience
major_events_or_movements.description: Questions about fasting lead to calls for justice, mercy, and sincere covenant life.

major_events_or_movements.title: Coming King and Future Day
major_events_or_movements.description: Later oracles portray a humble king, a pierced figure, purification, conflict, and the LORD reigning over all.

key_figures.name: Zechariah
key_figures.description: A prophet and priest who receives night visions and encourages temple rebuilding.

key_figures.name: Joshua the high priest
key_figures.description: Pictured in a vision being cleansed and reclothed, and later symbolically crowned.

key_figures.name: Zerubbabel
key_figures.description: The governor promised that the temple will be finished 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.'

key_figures.name: The Accuser (Satan)
key_figures.description: Stands to accuse Joshua in the vision and is rebuked by the LORD.

key_figures.name: The interpreting angel
key_figures.description: Explains the meaning of Zechariah's visions.

key_figures.name: The humble king
key_figures.description: A coming king who enters Jerusalem on a donkey; the Gospels apply this to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.

key_figures.name: The pierced one
key_figures.description: A figure whom the people look upon and mourn, which John's Gospel connects with Jesus' crucifixion.

books.interpretive_notes: Zechariah contains highly symbolic prophecy, and Christian traditions differ substantially over the timing and fulfillment of many passages.

books.name: Malachi
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally understood as Malachi; the Hebrew name can also mean 'my messenger,' so some scholars consider whether it functions as a title.
books.original_audience: The post-exilic Jewish community in Judah.
books.purpose: To confront spiritual apathy, corrupt worship, covenant unfaithfulness, and doubts about God's justice while calling the people back to faithful worship and obedience.
books.historical_context: Malachi is generally placed in the Persian-period post-exilic era, often in the fifth century BC. The temple is functioning, but the community is discouraged and spiritually careless.
books.overall_theme: God remains faithful to His covenant and calls His people to return to sincere worship and faithful obedience while awaiting His coming judgment and restoration.
books.plain_english_summary: Malachi addresses a community that has returned from exile but become cynical and careless. Priests offer unacceptable sacrifices, relationships are unfaithful, giving is neglected, and people question whether serving God matters. The book closes with a coming messenger and the day of the LORD.

major_events_or_movements.title: Corrupt Worship Confronted
major_events_or_movements.description: God affirms His love for Israel, then rebukes the priests for offering defective sacrifices and dishonoring His name.

major_events_or_movements.title: Covenant Unfaithfulness Rebuked
major_events_or_movements.description: The people are confronted over broken faith in worship, marriage, and community life.

major_events_or_movements.title: Coming Messenger and Return to God
major_events_or_movements.description: God promises a messenger, calls the people to return in faithfulness, and points toward the day of the LORD.

key_figures.name: Malachi
key_figures.description: The prophet ('my messenger') who confronts the post-exilic community.

key_figures.name: The priests
key_figures.description: Rebuked for offering blemished sacrifices and failing to teach faithfully.

key_figures.name: Jacob and Esau
key_figures.description: Recalled to illustrate God's covenant love for Israel.

key_figures.name: The messenger
key_figures.description: One who will prepare the way before the LORD; the Gospels identify him with John the Baptist.

key_figures.name: Elijah
key_figures.description: The prophet promised to come before the great day of the LORD to turn hearts.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians identify the messenger-preparing-the-way language with John the Baptist; views differ on whether Elijah language also points to an additional future fulfillment.

books.name: Matthew
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Matthew, the tax collector and apostle; the Gospel itself is formally anonymous.
books.original_audience: A largely Jewish-Christian audience, while addressing the wider mission to all nations.
books.purpose: To present Jesus as Messiah, Son of David, new-Moses-like teacher, and fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures, culminating in the mission to make disciples of all nations.
books.historical_context: Written in the first-century Roman world after Jesus' ministry, Matthew frequently engages Jewish Scripture, law, and messianic expectation.
books.overall_theme: Jesus is Israel's Messiah and authoritative King who fulfills Scripture and forms a disciple community for all nations.
books.plain_english_summary: Matthew traces Jesus from Abraham and David through His teaching, miracles, conflict, death, and resurrection, emphasizing fulfillment of Scripture and the demands of discipleship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Birth and Early Ministry
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus' genealogy, birth, baptism, temptation, and beginning ministry establish His messianic identity.

major_events_or_movements.title: Teaching and Kingdom Ministry
major_events_or_movements.description: The Sermon on the Mount and later teaching blocks explain kingdom life while miracles display Jesus' authority.

major_events_or_movements.title: Death, Resurrection, and Great Commission
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus is crucified, raised, and commissions disciples to make disciples of all nations.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The Messiah, Son of David and Son of God, whose teaching, death, and resurrection are the center of the Gospel.

key_figures.name: Mary
key_figures.description: The mother of Jesus, who conceives by the Holy Spirit.

key_figures.name: Joseph
key_figures.description: Mary's husband, a descendant of David, guided by dreams to protect the child.

key_figures.name: The magi
key_figures.description: Wise men from the east who follow a star to worship the newborn king.

key_figures.name: Herod the Great
key_figures.description: King of Judea who tries to kill the infant Jesus.

key_figures.name: John the Baptist
key_figures.description: The prophet who prepares the way for Jesus and baptizes Him.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: Leader among the twelve disciples, who confesses Jesus as the Messiah but later denies Him.

key_figures.name: Judas Iscariot
key_figures.description: The disciple who betrays Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.

key_figures.name: Caiaphas
key_figures.description: The high priest who presides at Jesus' trial before the council.

key_figures.name: Pontius Pilate
key_figures.description: The Roman governor who sentences Jesus to crucifixion.

key_figures.name: Mary Magdalene
key_figures.description: A follower of Jesus who witnesses His death and the empty tomb.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians agree on Matthew's central portrayal of Jesus as Messiah, though details of prophecy fulfillment and end-times teaching are interpreted differently across traditions.

books.name: Mark
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to John Mark, associated with Peter; the Gospel itself is anonymous.
books.original_audience: Likely Gentile Christians, often associated by tradition with Rome.
books.purpose: To present Jesus as the powerful yet suffering Son of God and to define discipleship through the cross.
books.historical_context: Mark reflects a first-century Roman setting and explains some Jewish customs and Aramaic expressions for readers who may not know them.
books.overall_theme: Jesus' identity is revealed through authority, suffering, death, and resurrection; His followers are called to costly discipleship.
books.plain_english_summary: Mark moves quickly through Jesus' ministry, repeatedly asking who He really is. The turning point comes when Jesus explains that Messiahship leads through suffering and the cross.

major_events_or_movements.title: Authority in Galilee
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus teaches, heals, exorcises, and gathers disciples with striking authority.

major_events_or_movements.title: Confession and Way of the Cross
major_events_or_movements.description: Peter confesses Jesus as Messiah, after which Jesus repeatedly teaches about suffering and discipleship.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jerusalem, Crucifixion, and Resurrection
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus enters Jerusalem, confronts leaders, is crucified, and the tomb is found empty.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The Son of God and suffering Messiah, whose authority and self-giving death drive the Gospel.

key_figures.name: John the Baptist
key_figures.description: The forerunner who prepares the way and is later executed by Herod Antipas.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: A leading disciple who confesses Jesus as the Christ but denies Him during the trial.

key_figures.name: James and John
key_figures.description: The sons of Zebedee, part of Jesus' inner circle, who ask for places of honor.

key_figures.name: Herod Antipas
key_figures.description: Ruler of Galilee who has John the Baptist beheaded.

key_figures.name: Bartimaeus
key_figures.description: A blind beggar near Jericho who receives his sight and follows Jesus.

key_figures.name: Judas Iscariot
key_figures.description: The disciple who betrays Jesus to the chief priests.

key_figures.name: Pontius Pilate
key_figures.description: The Roman governor who hands Jesus over to be crucified.

key_figures.name: Joseph of Arimathea
key_figures.description: A council member who boldly asks for Jesus' body and buries Him.

key_figures.name: Mary Magdalene
key_figures.description: Among the women who witness the crucifixion and find the tomb empty.

books.interpretive_notes: The earliest manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8; later manuscripts contain longer endings. Modern Bibles usually note this textual issue.

books.name: Luke
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Luke, a physician and companion of Paul; the Gospel itself is anonymous but is paired with Acts by the same author.
books.original_audience: Theophilus and a broader Gentile-Christian audience.
books.purpose: To provide an orderly account of Jesus' life and show God's salvation extending to the marginalized and ultimately to all nations.
books.historical_context: Luke writes in the first-century Greco-Roman world and carefully situates events among rulers, places, and Jewish religious life.
books.overall_theme: In Jesus, God's promised salvation comes for Israel and reaches outward to all peoples, especially the overlooked and excluded.
books.plain_english_summary: Luke presents Jesus as Spirit-anointed Savior, teacher, prophet, and Son of Man. It highlights prayer, the Holy Spirit, women, the poor, outsiders, and the journey toward Jerusalem.

major_events_or_movements.title: Birth Narratives and Preparation
major_events_or_movements.description: The births of John the Baptist and Jesus are announced and connected to Israel's hopes; Jesus is baptized, tempted, and announces His mission in Nazareth.

major_events_or_movements.title: Ministry and Journey to Jerusalem
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus teaches, heals, welcomes outsiders, and tells distinctive parables while moving toward Jerusalem.

major_events_or_movements.title: Death, Resurrection, and Ascension
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus is crucified, raised, appears to disciples, and ascends, preparing for the continuation in Acts.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The Spirit-anointed Savior who seeks and saves the lost and brings good news to the poor.

key_figures.name: Theophilus
key_figures.description: The person to whom Luke addresses his orderly account.

key_figures.name: Zechariah and Elizabeth
key_figures.description: An elderly priestly couple who become the parents of John the Baptist.

key_figures.name: Mary
key_figures.description: The mother of Jesus, who receives Gabriel's announcement and sings the Magnificat.

key_figures.name: John the Baptist
key_figures.description: The prophet who calls Israel to repentance and prepares the way for Jesus.

key_figures.name: Simeon and Anna
key_figures.description: Devout elders who recognize the infant Jesus in the temple.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: A fisherman called to follow Jesus, who later denies Him and is restored.

key_figures.name: Mary and Martha
key_figures.description: Sisters who welcome Jesus into their home.

key_figures.name: Zacchaeus
key_figures.description: A chief tax collector in Jericho transformed by Jesus' visit.

key_figures.name: Pontius Pilate and Herod Antipas
key_figures.description: The Roman governor and the ruler of Galilee who examine Jesus at His trial.

key_figures.name: Cleopas
key_figures.description: One of two disciples who meet the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus.

books.interpretive_notes: Luke shares much material with Matthew and Mark, and scholars debate the exact relationships among the Synoptic Gospels; Luke's prologue (1:1-4) explicitly describes using earlier sources and eyewitness testimony.

books.name: John
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to John the apostle; the Gospel refers to the 'beloved disciple' and likely reflects testimony preserved within a Johannine community.
books.original_audience: A broad Christian audience, including readers facing questions about Jesus' identity and faith.
books.purpose: To lead readers to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and to have life in His name.
books.historical_context: John reflects the first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman world but is organized differently from the Synoptic Gospels, emphasizing signs, extended discourses, and festival settings.
books.overall_theme: Jesus is the eternal Word made flesh who reveals the Father and gives eternal life to those who believe.
books.plain_english_summary: John opens with Jesus as the eternal Word and structures much of the story around signs and 'I am' sayings. The Gospel climaxes in Jesus' death and resurrection as the decisive revelation of divine glory and life.

major_events_or_movements.title: Signs and Public Ministry
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus performs signs such as turning water to wine, healing, feeding the multitude, and raising Lazarus.

major_events_or_movements.title: Farewell Teaching
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus prepares His disciples for His departure, promising the Holy Spirit and calling them to love and abide in Him.

major_events_or_movements.title: Passion and Resurrection
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus is crucified, buried, raised, and appears to disciples including Thomas and Peter.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The eternal Word made flesh, who reveals the Father through signs, 'I am' sayings, death, and resurrection.

key_figures.name: John the Baptist
key_figures.description: Testifies that Jesus is the Lamb of God.

key_figures.name: Nicodemus
key_figures.description: A Pharisee who comes to Jesus at night and later helps bury Him.

key_figures.name: The Samaritan woman
key_figures.description: Meets Jesus at a well and brings her town to hear Him.

key_figures.name: Lazarus, Martha, and Mary
key_figures.description: Siblings from Bethany; Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: Leading disciple who denies Jesus and is restored by Him after the resurrection.

key_figures.name: The beloved disciple
key_figures.description: The disciple whom Jesus loved, whose testimony stands behind the Gospel.

key_figures.name: Thomas
key_figures.description: The disciple who doubts the resurrection until he sees Jesus and confesses, 'My Lord and my God.'

key_figures.name: Caiaphas
key_figures.description: The high priest who says it is better for one man to die for the people.

key_figures.name: Pontius Pilate
key_figures.description: The Roman governor who asks 'What is truth?' and hands Jesus over to be crucified.

key_figures.name: Mary Magdalene
key_figures.description: The first to meet the risen Jesus at the tomb.

books.interpretive_notes: Christian traditions broadly affirm John's high Christology, while debates continue over the precise historical and theological relationship between John and the Synoptic Gospels.

books.name: Acts
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Luke, author of the Gospel of Luke.
books.original_audience: Theophilus and the wider church.
books.purpose: To show how the risen Jesus continues His mission through the Holy Spirit as the gospel moves from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the wider Roman world.
books.historical_context: Acts is set in the first-century Roman Empire and covers the church's expansion from Jerusalem to Rome.
books.overall_theme: The Holy Spirit empowers the church to bear witness to Jesus across ethnic, geographic, and social boundaries.
books.plain_english_summary: Acts begins with Jesus' ascension and Pentecost, follows the Jerusalem church and persecution, then shifts toward Paul's missionary journeys and eventual arrival in Rome.

major_events_or_movements.title: Pentecost and Jerusalem Church
major_events_or_movements.description: The Holy Spirit is poured out, Peter preaches, and a new community forms.

major_events_or_movements.title: Gospel Expands Beyond Jerusalem
major_events_or_movements.description: Persecution scatters believers, Samaritans receive the message, Saul is converted, and Peter is sent to the Gentile Cornelius.

major_events_or_movements.title: Paul's Missions and Journey to Rome
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul carries the gospel across the eastern Mediterranean and eventually reaches Rome as a prisoner.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The risen Lord who ascends and continues His work through the Spirit and His witnesses.

key_figures.name: Theophilus
key_figures.description: The person to whom Luke addresses the book.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: Preaches at Pentecost, leads the Jerusalem church, and brings the gospel to Cornelius.

key_figures.name: John
key_figures.description: Peter's companion in early ministry and before the council.

key_figures.name: Stephen
key_figures.description: One of the seven, who becomes the first Christian martyr.

key_figures.name: Philip
key_figures.description: One of the seven, who preaches in Samaria and baptizes the Ethiopian official.

key_figures.name: Paul (Saul)
key_figures.description: A persecutor converted on the road to Damascus, who becomes the great missionary to the Gentiles.

key_figures.name: Barnabas
key_figures.description: An encourager who sponsors Paul and joins him on the first missionary journey.

key_figures.name: Cornelius
key_figures.description: A God-fearing Roman centurion whose household receives the Spirit.

key_figures.name: James
key_figures.description: The brother of Jesus and a leader of the Jerusalem church at the council in Acts 15.

key_figures.name: Silas, Timothy, and Luke
key_figures.description: Paul's coworkers on later journeys; Luke appears in the 'we' passages.

key_figures.name: Lydia
key_figures.description: A merchant in Philippi who becomes the first recorded convert in Europe.

key_figures.name: Priscilla and Aquila
key_figures.description: A married couple who work with Paul and instruct Apollos.

key_figures.name: Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
key_figures.description: Roman officials and a Jewish king before whom Paul defends himself.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians differ on how certain events in Acts, especially signs, tongues, and Spirit reception patterns, should function normatively in the church today.

books.name: Romans
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle.
books.original_audience: Christians in Rome, including both Jewish and Gentile believers.
books.purpose: To explain the gospel, address tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers, and prepare for Paul's hoped-for mission farther west.
books.historical_context: Romans was written in the mid-first century, likely from Corinth, to a church probably shaped by the return of Jewish believers after Emperor Claudius' expulsion of Jews from Rome.
books.overall_theme: God's righteousness is revealed in the gospel: all have sinned, justification is by faith, new life comes through the Spirit, and Jews and Gentiles are united in God's saving plan.
books.plain_english_summary: Romans gives Paul's fullest sustained explanation of the gospel, moving from universal sin to justification, new life, Israel's place in God's purposes, and practical life in a diverse church.

major_events_or_movements.title: Human Sin and Justification
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul argues that both Gentiles and Jews are under sin and that justification comes through faith apart from works of the law.

major_events_or_movements.title: New Life in Christ and the Spirit
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are united with Christ, freed from sin's dominion, and empowered by the Spirit.

major_events_or_movements.title: Israel, Church Unity, and Christian Practice
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul wrestles with Israel's place in God's plan and calls the Roman church to humble, unified, sacrificial living.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: The apostle writing to a church he has not yet visited.

key_figures.name: Abraham
key_figures.description: Presented as the father of all who believe, justified by faith before circumcision.

key_figures.name: Adam
key_figures.description: Contrasted with Christ: through Adam came sin and death, through Christ grace and life.

key_figures.name: Phoebe
key_figures.description: A servant (or deacon) of the church at Cenchreae, likely the letter's carrier.

key_figures.name: Priscilla and Aquila
key_figures.description: Coworkers of Paul who risked their lives for him and host a church.

key_figures.name: Tertius
key_figures.description: The scribe who wrote down the letter.

books.interpretive_notes: Christian traditions differ on questions such as justification, predestination, Israel and the church, and the relationship between faith and works, so disputed interpretations should be presented with care.

books.name: 1 Corinthians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle.
books.original_audience: The church in Corinth.
books.purpose: To correct divisions, immorality, lawsuits, disorderly worship, and confusion about marriage, spiritual gifts, the Lord's Supper, and resurrection.
books.historical_context: Corinth was a wealthy, diverse Greco-Roman city known for commerce, status competition, and multiple religious traditions.
books.overall_theme: The cross reshapes Christian identity, relationships, worship, freedom, and hope.
books.plain_english_summary: Paul responds to reports and questions from a gifted but divided church. He repeatedly redirects believers from status and self-interest toward holiness, love, mutual edification, and resurrection hope.

major_events_or_movements.title: Divisions and Moral Problems Addressed
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul confronts factions, pride, sexual immorality, and lawsuits.

major_events_or_movements.title: Questions about Christian Life and Worship
major_events_or_movements.description: Marriage, food offered to idols, the Lord's Supper, head coverings, and spiritual gifts are discussed.

major_events_or_movements.title: Resurrection Defended
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul insists that bodily resurrection is central to the gospel and Christian hope.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: The church's founder, writing to correct and instruct it.

key_figures.name: Sosthenes
key_figures.description: Named as co-sender of the letter.

key_figures.name: Apollos
key_figures.description: A gifted teacher whom some in Corinth set up as a rival to Paul.

key_figures.name: Cephas (Peter)
key_figures.description: Another leader around whom a faction forms.

key_figures.name: Chloe's people
key_figures.description: Members of a household who report the church's quarrels to Paul.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Paul's coworker, sent to remind the church of Paul's ways.

key_figures.name: Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus
key_figures.description: Corinthian believers who visit Paul and refresh his spirit.

books.interpretive_notes: Passages on gender roles, spiritual gifts, and worship practices are interpreted differently across Christian traditions.

books.name: 2 Corinthians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle.
books.original_audience: The church in Corinth.
books.purpose: To defend Paul's apostolic ministry, explain the character of Christian ministry, encourage reconciliation, and complete a collection for believers in Jerusalem.
books.historical_context: The letter reflects a strained relationship between Paul and Corinth, including criticism from rival teachers and a painful earlier visit or correspondence.
books.overall_theme: God's power is displayed through weakness, suffering, integrity, generosity, and reconciliation.
books.plain_english_summary: Paul speaks with unusual personal openness about suffering, ministry, reconciliation, generosity, and his contested relationship with the Corinthians.

major_events_or_movements.title: Ministry through Weakness
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul explains affliction, comfort, integrity, and the treasure of the gospel in fragile human vessels.

major_events_or_movements.title: Collection for Jerusalem
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul urges generous, willing participation in relief for needy believers.

major_events_or_movements.title: Defense of Apostleship
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul confronts rival claims and argues that true apostolic authority is marked by suffering, weakness, and dependence on Christ.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Defends his ministry and expresses deep affection for the church.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Named as co-sender.

key_figures.name: Titus
key_figures.description: Paul's coworker who brings encouraging news from Corinth and helps organize the collection.

key_figures.name: The 'super-apostles'
key_figures.description: Rival teachers who boast in credentials and undermine Paul.

key_figures.name: The offender
key_figures.description: An unnamed person disciplined by the church whom Paul now urges them to forgive.

books.interpretive_notes: Many scholars think 2 Corinthians may combine more than one letter, especially because of the sharp change in tone at chapter 10, while others defend its unity; Paul also refers to a 'severe letter' that may not have survived.

books.name: Galatians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle.
books.original_audience: Churches in Galatia; the exact geographic identification is debated.
books.purpose: To oppose pressure on Gentile believers to adopt circumcision and law observance as necessary for covenant inclusion and to defend justification by faith in Christ.
books.historical_context: The letter arises from controversy over how Gentiles enter God's people in the early church.
books.overall_theme: In Christ, people are justified by faith and live by the Spirit rather than relying on works of the law for covenant status.
books.plain_english_summary: Paul strongly defends the gospel he preached, argues from Abraham and Scripture, and calls believers to use freedom not for self-indulgence but for Spirit-shaped love.

major_events_or_movements.title: Paul Defends His Gospel
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul recounts his calling and confrontations over Gentile inclusion.

major_events_or_movements.title: Faith, Promise, and Law
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul argues that God's promise to Abraham precedes the law and that justification comes through faith.

major_events_or_movements.title: Freedom and Life in the Spirit
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are called to stand firm in freedom and bear the fruit of the Spirit through love.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Defends the gospel of grace and his apostolic calling.

key_figures.name: Peter (Cephas)
key_figures.description: Confronted by Paul at Antioch for withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentiles.

key_figures.name: James
key_figures.description: The Lord's brother and a pillar of the Jerusalem church.

key_figures.name: Barnabas
key_figures.description: Paul's companion, who is briefly drawn into the withdrawal at Antioch.

key_figures.name: Titus
key_figures.description: A Gentile believer who was not compelled to be circumcised.

key_figures.name: Abraham
key_figures.description: Paul's chief example of justification by faith and the recipient of the promise.

key_figures.name: Hagar and Sarah
key_figures.description: Used in an allegory contrasting slavery and freedom.

books.interpretive_notes: Christian traditions differ on the precise meaning of 'works of the law' and aspects of justification, though all recognize the letter's central concern with faith in Christ and Gentile inclusion.

books.name: Ephesians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Paul; some modern scholars debate Pauline authorship.
books.original_audience: Christians in and around Ephesus, possibly intended as a circular letter for multiple churches.
books.purpose: To describe God's cosmic plan in Christ and call the church to live in unity, holiness, love, and spiritual strength.
books.historical_context: Ephesus was a major Roman city and religious center in Asia Minor. The letter addresses a largely Gentile church context.
books.overall_theme: God unites all things in Christ and creates one new people who should live in unity, holiness, love, and spiritual maturity.
books.plain_english_summary: Ephesians moves from what God has done in Christ—election, redemption, grace, reconciliation—to how believers should live as one body, one family, and one people equipped for spiritual conflict.

major_events_or_movements.title: Spiritual Blessings in Christ
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul praises God's saving purpose and grace in Christ.

major_events_or_movements.title: Jew and Gentile United
major_events_or_movements.description: Christ's work creates one new humanity and one household of God.

major_events_or_movements.title: Walk Worthy and Stand Firm
major_events_or_movements.description: The church is called to unity, holiness, transformed relationships, and spiritual armor.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes as a prisoner for the Lord.

key_figures.name: Tychicus
key_figures.description: A faithful minister sent to carry the letter and report on Paul.

books.interpretive_notes: Debates include authorship and the application of household codes, but the letter's emphasis on unity in Christ is widely shared.

books.name: Philippians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle, writing with Timothy named in the greeting.
books.original_audience: The church in Philippi.
books.purpose: To thank the Philippians for support, encourage unity and joy amid suffering, and present Christ's humility as the pattern for Christian life.
books.historical_context: Paul writes from imprisonment; the exact location is debated. Philippi was a Roman colony with strong civic identity.
books.overall_theme: Joy and faithful unity are possible in suffering when believers center life on Christ's humility, resurrection, and coming victory.
books.plain_english_summary: Philippians is a warm letter of gratitude and encouragement. Paul discusses imprisonment, Christ's self-emptying humility, warnings against false confidence, and contentment in every circumstance.

major_events_or_movements.title: Gospel Advances through Imprisonment
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul explains that his confinement has unexpectedly helped spread the gospel.

major_events_or_movements.title: Christ's Humility as the Model
major_events_or_movements.description: The famous Christ hymn calls believers to self-giving unity and obedience.

major_events_or_movements.title: Pressing On and Learning Contentment
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul rejects confidence in status, pursues Christ, and explains contentment in plenty or need.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes from imprisonment with joy and gratitude.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Co-sender, commended for genuine concern for the church.

key_figures.name: Epaphroditus
key_figures.description: The Philippians' messenger to Paul, who nearly died in service.

key_figures.name: Euodia and Syntyche
key_figures.description: Two women who labored with Paul and are urged to agree in the Lord.

books.interpretive_notes: The location of Paul's imprisonment (Rome, Ephesus, or Caesarea) affects the letter's date; Christian traditions differ on how to understand the self-emptying of Christ in Philippians 2:7.

books.name: Colossians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Paul, with Timothy named in the greeting; some modern scholars debate Pauline authorship.
books.original_audience: The church in Colossae.
books.purpose: To affirm the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ and warn against teachings that diminish His centrality.
books.historical_context: Colossae was a smaller city in Asia Minor. The letter responds to pressures involving philosophy, asceticism, visions, calendar observance, and spiritual powers.
books.overall_theme: Christ is supreme over creation and the church, and believers are complete in Him.
books.plain_english_summary: Colossians presents an exalted picture of Christ, warns against spiritual systems that promise fullness elsewhere, and calls believers to put off the old life and put on a Christlike one.

major_events_or_movements.title: Supremacy of Christ
major_events_or_movements.description: A major hymn presents Christ as image of the invisible God, creator, sustainer, and head of the church.

major_events_or_movements.title: Warnings against Rival Spiritual Claims
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are told not to be captured by teachings centered on regulations, asceticism, or angelic powers.

major_events_or_movements.title: New Life in Christ
major_events_or_movements.description: Practical exhortations address character, relationships, households, prayer, and witness.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes from prison to a church he has not visited.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Named as co-sender.

key_figures.name: Epaphras
key_figures.description: Founder of the Colossian church, who prays earnestly for them.

key_figures.name: Tychicus and Onesimus
key_figures.description: Sent to deliver the letter and report on Paul.

key_figures.name: Aristarchus, Mark, Luke, and Demas
key_figures.description: Companions of Paul who send greetings.

key_figures.name: Archippus
key_figures.description: Encouraged to complete the ministry he has received.

books.interpretive_notes: The precise nature of the false teaching at Colossae is debated, with proposals including Jewish mysticism, early Gnostic ideas, or local folk religion; Colossians has close parallels with Ephesians.

books.name: 1 Thessalonians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle, with Silvanus and Timothy named in the greeting.
books.original_audience: The church in Thessalonica.
books.purpose: To encourage a young persecuted church, affirm their faith, call for holy living, and clarify hope concerning believers who had died before Christ's return.
books.historical_context: Thessalonica was a major Macedonian city. The church formed during a brief and contentious missionary stay.
books.overall_theme: Faithful Christian life combines hope in Christ's return, holiness, mutual love, and perseverance under pressure.
books.plain_english_summary: Paul warmly remembers the Thessalonians' conversion, encourages sexual holiness and brotherly love, and reassures them that deceased believers will share fully in Christ's return.

major_events_or_movements.title: Conversion and Perseverance Remembered
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul recalls the church's turning from idols and endurance under persecution.

major_events_or_movements.title: Holy Living Encouraged
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are called to sexual holiness, brotherly love, and responsible work.

major_events_or_movements.title: Hope in Christ's Return
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul comforts the church regarding deceased believers and urges readiness for the day of the Lord.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes with deep affection to a young church he had to leave abruptly.

key_figures.name: Silvanus (Silas)
key_figures.description: Paul's coworker in founding the church; named as co-sender.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Sent back to strengthen the church; returns with a good report of their faith and love.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians differ on the timing and sequence of end-times events associated with Christ's return, so the passage should not be reduced to one disputed system.

books.name: 2 Thessalonians
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy named in the greeting; authorship is debated by some modern scholars.
books.original_audience: The church in Thessalonica.
books.purpose: To encourage persecuted believers, correct confusion about the day of the Lord, and address idleness within the community.
books.historical_context: The letter follows ongoing pressure on the Thessalonian church and apparent misunderstanding of Paul's earlier teaching about Christ's return.
books.overall_theme: Persevere faithfully, do not be deceived about the end, and continue responsible Christian living.
books.plain_english_summary: 2 Thessalonians reassures suffering believers that God will judge evil, warns that certain events must precede the day of the Lord, and commands disorderly members to work quietly.

major_events_or_movements.title: Perseverance under Persecution
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul praises endurance and points toward God's righteous judgment.

major_events_or_movements.title: Correction about the Day of the Lord
major_events_or_movements.description: The church is told not to panic and is given difficult teaching about rebellion and the 'man of lawlessness.'

major_events_or_movements.title: Work and Discipline
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul addresses those who have become idle and disruptive.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes to correct confusion about the day of the Lord.

key_figures.name: Silvanus and Timothy
key_figures.description: Named as co-senders.

key_figures.name: The man of lawlessness
key_figures.description: A figure of rebellion who must be revealed before the day of the Lord.

books.interpretive_notes: The identity and timing of the 'man of lawlessness' and related end-times events are interpreted differently across Christian traditions.

books.name: 1 Timothy
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Paul and addressed to Timothy; some modern scholars debate Pauline authorship.
books.original_audience: Timothy in Ephesus and the churches under his care.
books.purpose: To guide church order, sound teaching, leadership qualifications, worship, care for vulnerable members, and faithful ministry.
books.historical_context: The letter addresses false teaching and community order in the Ephesian church context.
books.overall_theme: Healthy churches require sound teaching, godly leadership, disciplined care, and lives that match the gospel.
books.plain_english_summary: 1 Timothy combines pastoral guidance with instructions about doctrine, prayer, leadership, widows, elders, money, and Timothy's own conduct.

major_events_or_movements.title: False Teaching Confronted
major_events_or_movements.description: Timothy is urged to resist speculative teaching and preserve the gospel's aim of love and good conscience.

major_events_or_movements.title: Worship and Leadership Ordered
major_events_or_movements.description: Instructions address prayer, men and women in worship, overseers, and deacons.

major_events_or_movements.title: Pastoral Care and Godly Conduct
major_events_or_movements.description: The letter covers widows, elders, wealth, discipline, and Timothy's example.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes to instruct his coworker on church life and leadership.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Paul's 'true child in the faith,' left in Ephesus to confront false teaching.

key_figures.name: Hymenaeus and Alexander
key_figures.description: Men who have shipwrecked their faith and been disciplined.

books.interpretive_notes: Passages about church offices and gender roles are interpreted differently across Christian traditions.

books.name: 2 Timothy
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Paul and addressed to Timothy; some modern scholars debate Pauline authorship.
books.original_audience: Timothy, with wider relevance for church leaders and believers.
books.purpose: To strengthen Timothy for faithful ministry amid suffering, false teaching, and Paul's approaching death.
books.historical_context: The letter presents Paul as imprisoned and expecting execution, giving it the tone of a final charge.
books.overall_theme: Guard the gospel, endure suffering, handle Scripture faithfully, and finish the race with perseverance.
books.plain_english_summary: 2 Timothy is personal and urgent. Paul calls Timothy to courage, disciplined endurance, faithful teaching, Scripture-shaped ministry, and confidence that the gospel cannot be imprisoned.

major_events_or_movements.title: Guard the Gospel
major_events_or_movements.description: Timothy is urged not to be ashamed and to entrust sound teaching to reliable people.

major_events_or_movements.title: Difficult Times and Scripture
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul warns about corrupt teachers and highlights the usefulness of God-breathed Scripture.

major_events_or_movements.title: Final Charge and Farewell
major_events_or_movements.description: Timothy is told to preach the word; Paul reflects that he has fought the good fight and finished the race.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes from prison, expecting his death, with a final charge.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Urged to guard the gospel and endure suffering.

key_figures.name: Lois and Eunice
key_figures.description: Timothy's grandmother and mother, known for their sincere faith.

key_figures.name: Onesiphorus
key_figures.description: Searched for Paul in Rome and was not ashamed of his chains.

key_figures.name: Hymenaeus and Philetus
key_figures.description: Teachers who claim the resurrection has already happened.

key_figures.name: Demas
key_figures.description: A coworker who deserts Paul because he loves this present world.

key_figures.name: Luke and Mark
key_figures.description: Luke alone remains with Paul; Mark is requested as useful for ministry.

key_figures.name: Alexander the coppersmith
key_figures.description: A man who did Paul great harm and opposed his message.

books.interpretive_notes: 2 Timothy 3:16 is a central text in Christian discussions of the inspiration and authority of Scripture; traditions differ in how they articulate the nature of that inspiration.

books.name: Titus
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Paul and addressed to Titus; some modern scholars debate Pauline authorship.
books.original_audience: Titus and churches in Crete.
books.purpose: To organize churches with qualified leaders, oppose false teaching, and connect sound doctrine with good works.
books.historical_context: Crete had a reputation in ancient literature for moral and social problems, and the churches needed stable leadership.
books.overall_theme: Grace trains God's people to live self-controlled, upright, productive lives that make the gospel attractive.
books.plain_english_summary: Titus instructs the appointment of elders, correction of false teachers, practical teaching for different groups, and a strong emphasis on good works flowing from grace.

major_events_or_movements.title: Elders Appointed
major_events_or_movements.description: Titus is instructed to establish qualified leadership in Cretan churches.

major_events_or_movements.title: Sound Doctrine Produces Godly Living
major_events_or_movements.description: Different age and social groups are taught conduct consistent with grace.

major_events_or_movements.title: Grace and Good Works
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are reminded that salvation comes by God's mercy and should result in lives devoted to doing good.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes to guide the organization of churches in Crete.

key_figures.name: Titus
key_figures.description: Paul's coworker, left in Crete to appoint elders and teach sound doctrine.

key_figures.name: Zenas and Apollos
key_figures.description: A lawyer and a teacher whom Titus is asked to help on their journey.

key_figures.name: Artemas and Tychicus
key_figures.description: Coworkers, one of whom Paul plans to send so Titus can join him at Nicopolis.

books.interpretive_notes: Titus 1:12 quotes a Cretan poet, usually identified as Epimenides; readers should take the quotation as Paul's use of a well-known saying rather than as a blanket judgment on an ethnic group.

books.name: Philemon
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Paul the apostle, with Timothy named in the greeting.
books.original_audience: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church meeting in Philemon's house.
books.purpose: To appeal for Onesimus, asking Philemon to receive him not merely as a slave but as a beloved brother in Christ.
books.historical_context: The letter is set within the Roman slave system, in which enslaved people had limited legal standing and household relationships were highly unequal.
books.overall_theme: The gospel transforms relationships by creating a new family identity in Christ that challenges status and demands costly reconciliation.
books.plain_english_summary: Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon with a personal appeal grounded in love rather than coercion. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself.

major_events_or_movements.title: Paul Gives Thanks for Philemon
major_events_or_movements.description: The letter opens by praising Philemon's love and faith.

major_events_or_movements.title: Appeal for Onesimus
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul pleads for Onesimus, now described as useful and beloved in the Lord.

major_events_or_movements.title: Receive Him as You Would Me
major_events_or_movements.description: Paul offers to cover any debt and appeals for reconciled fellowship.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Writes from prison with a personal appeal.

key_figures.name: Philemon
key_figures.description: A believer who hosts a church in his house and is Onesimus' master.

key_figures.name: Onesimus
key_figures.description: An enslaved man who has become a believer and whom Paul sends back as a brother.

key_figures.name: Apphia and Archippus
key_figures.description: Members of Philemon's household church, greeted in the opening.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Named as co-sender.

key_figures.name: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke
key_figures.description: Paul's companions who send greetings.

books.interpretive_notes: Christians differ on how directly Philemon challenges slavery as an institution, but the letter clearly reframes master-slave relations around Christian brotherhood.

books.name: Hebrews
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Anonymous; early Christians proposed various authors, but the text does not identify its writer.
books.original_audience: Christians under pressure who appear tempted to drift from their confession.
books.purpose: To show the supremacy of Christ, the sufficiency of His priesthood and sacrifice, and the need for persevering faith.
books.historical_context: Hebrews assumes deep familiarity with Israel's Scriptures, priesthood, sacrifices, wilderness story, and covenant themes.
books.overall_theme: Jesus is the definitive Son, high priest, and sacrifice; therefore believers must hold fast in faith and draw near to God.
books.plain_english_summary: Hebrews compares Jesus with angels, Moses, priests, and sacrifices, arguing that He fulfills and surpasses them all. Strong warnings against drifting are paired with encouragement to endure by faith.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Son Is Supreme
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus is presented as greater than angels and Moses and as the faithful Son over God's house.

major_events_or_movements.title: Superior High Priest and Sacrifice
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus' priesthood is associated with Melchizedek, and His once-for-all sacrifice inaugurates the new covenant.

major_events_or_movements.title: Perseverance by Faith
major_events_or_movements.description: Examples of faith and a call to run the race encourage readers to endure.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The Son and great high priest, shown to be superior to angels, Moses, and the Levitical priesthood.

key_figures.name: Moses
key_figures.description: Faithful as a servant in God's house, contrasted with Christ as the Son over it.

key_figures.name: Melchizedek
key_figures.description: The priest-king of Salem, whose priesthood foreshadows Christ's.

key_figures.name: Abraham
key_figures.description: An example of faith and patient endurance in receiving God's promise.

key_figures.name: The heroes of faith
key_figures.description: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and others listed in chapter 11.

key_figures.name: Timothy
key_figures.description: Mentioned at the close as recently released.

books.interpretive_notes: Christian traditions differ on how to interpret the warning passages, especially regarding apostasy and perseverance.

books.name: James
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to James, the brother of Jesus and leader in the Jerusalem church.
books.original_audience: The 'twelve tribes in the Dispersion,' understood as Jewish Christians scattered outside their homeland.
books.purpose: To call believers to mature, practical faith expressed through endurance, controlled speech, impartiality, generosity, wisdom, and prayer.
books.historical_context: The letter reflects Jewish wisdom traditions and addresses believers facing trials, economic inequality, and community conflict.
books.overall_theme: Genuine faith becomes visible in practical obedience, wisdom, mercy, and perseverance.
books.plain_english_summary: James is direct and practical. It urges believers to endure trials, do the word rather than merely hear it, avoid favoritism, control the tongue, reject selfish ambition, and pray faithfully.

major_events_or_movements.title: Trials and Doing the Word
major_events_or_movements.description: James connects testing with maturity and warns against hearing Scripture without obeying it.

major_events_or_movements.title: Faith, Works, and Impartiality
major_events_or_movements.description: Favoritism is condemned and living faith is distinguished from empty profession.

major_events_or_movements.title: Speech, Wisdom, Patience, and Prayer
major_events_or_movements.description: Later chapters address the tongue, conflict, wealth, patient endurance, confession, and prayer.

key_figures.name: James
key_figures.description: The author, traditionally the brother of Jesus and a leader of the Jerusalem church.

key_figures.name: Abraham
key_figures.description: Shows faith completed by works when he offers Isaac.

key_figures.name: Rahab
key_figures.description: Commended for faith shown in welcoming the spies.

key_figures.name: Job
key_figures.description: An example of steadfast endurance.

key_figures.name: Elijah
key_figures.description: An example of a person whose prayer was powerful and effective.

books.interpretive_notes: Christian traditions have sometimes differed in wording around faith and works, but James' focus is on the visible fruit of genuine faith rather than earning salvation by merit.

books.name: 1 Peter
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Peter the apostle; some modern scholars debate authorship.
books.original_audience: Christians scattered across provinces of Asia Minor.
books.purpose: To encourage believers facing social hostility and suffering to live holy, hopeful, honorable lives because of their new identity in Christ.
books.historical_context: The churches lived as religious minorities within the Roman world and faced pressure, slander, and exclusion.
books.overall_theme: Christians are a holy, pilgrim people whose hope in Christ enables faithful witness through suffering.
books.plain_english_summary: 1 Peter reminds believers of new birth and living hope, describes them as God's chosen people, and repeatedly connects Christ's suffering with patient, holy endurance.

major_events_or_movements.title: Living Hope and Holy Identity
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are reminded of new birth, future inheritance, and their calling as a holy people.

major_events_or_movements.title: Faithful Conduct amid Hostility
major_events_or_movements.description: Instructions address public life, households, suffering, and doing good.

major_events_or_movements.title: Shepherding and Endurance
major_events_or_movements.description: Elders are instructed to shepherd humbly, and the church is called to resist the devil and stand firm.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: The apostle writing to scattered believers facing suffering.

key_figures.name: Silvanus
key_figures.description: The faithful brother through whom Peter writes.

key_figures.name: Mark
key_figures.description: Called Peter's 'son,' sending greetings.

key_figures.name: Sarah
key_figures.description: Presented as an example of hope in God.

key_figures.name: Noah
key_figures.description: His family's rescue through water is compared with baptism.

books.interpretive_notes: Household passages and the nature of the suffering described are interpreted in different ways; applications should avoid endorsing abuse or coercion.

books.name: 2 Peter
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally attributed to Peter the apostle; authorship is widely debated in modern scholarship.
books.original_audience: Christians threatened by false teaching and skepticism about Christ's return.
books.purpose: To urge growth in godliness, oppose corrupt teachers, and reaffirm the certainty of the day of the Lord.
books.historical_context: The letter reflects an early Christian context in which some mock the expectation of Christ's return and distort moral freedom.
books.overall_theme: God's apparent delay is patience, not failure; believers should grow in holiness while awaiting final judgment and renewal.
books.plain_english_summary: 2 Peter urges believers to grow in virtue, recalls the apostolic witness to Christ's glory, warns strongly against false teachers, and responds to scoffers who deny coming judgment.

major_events_or_movements.title: Grow in Godliness
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are told to add virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, affection, and love to faith.

major_events_or_movements.title: False Teachers Condemned
major_events_or_movements.description: Corrupt teachers are described as greedy, sensual, and headed for judgment.

major_events_or_movements.title: The Day of the Lord Reaffirmed
major_events_or_movements.description: Scoffers are answered with an appeal to God's patience and a vision of future judgment and renewal.

key_figures.name: Peter
key_figures.description: Writes as an eyewitness of Christ's glory at the transfiguration, aware his death is near.

key_figures.name: Paul
key_figures.description: Called 'our beloved brother,' whose letters some twist.

key_figures.name: Noah and Lot
key_figures.description: Examples of the righteous whom God rescues amid judgment.

key_figures.name: Balaam
key_figures.description: An example of false teachers who love gain from wrongdoing.

books.interpretive_notes: 2 Peter shares extensive material with Jude, and its early reception in the church was slower than many New Testament books; it also refers to Paul's letters as Scripture (3:15-16).

books.name: 1 John
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Traditionally associated with John the apostle and the Johannine community; the letter itself is anonymous.
books.original_audience: Churches troubled by secession, false teaching, and uncertainty about genuine faith.
books.purpose: To give assurance of eternal life, defend the true confession of Jesus Christ, and emphasize obedience and love as marks of authentic Christian life.
books.historical_context: The letter reflects conflict within a Christian community over Christology, sin, authority, and fellowship.
books.overall_theme: True knowledge of God is shown by right belief about Jesus, obedience, and love for fellow believers.
books.plain_english_summary: 1 John repeatedly gives tests of authentic faith: confession of Jesus, walking in the light, obedience, love, and confidence in God's promise of eternal life.

major_events_or_movements.title: Walking in the Light
major_events_or_movements.description: God is light, sin must be confessed, and Christ is presented as advocate and atoning sacrifice.

major_events_or_movements.title: Children of God Love One Another
major_events_or_movements.description: The letter contrasts God's children with patterns of sin and hatred.

major_events_or_movements.title: Assurance of Eternal Life
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are given confidence grounded in faith in the Son and God's testimony.

key_figures.name: John (traditional author)
key_figures.description: Writes as one of the eyewitnesses who heard, saw, and touched the Word of life.

key_figures.name: The antichrists
key_figures.description: Those who have left the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh.

key_figures.name: Cain
key_figures.description: An example of hatred, contrasted with love for one another.

books.interpretive_notes: Traditions differ on how to relate the letter's strong statements about sinlessness to ongoing Christian struggle with sin; the letter itself also affirms confession and forgiveness.

books.name: 2 John
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Written by 'the elder,' traditionally associated with John the apostle.
books.original_audience: The 'elect lady and her children,' possibly an individual household or a local church.
books.purpose: To encourage truth and love while warning against supporting teachers who deny the true incarnation of Christ.
books.historical_context: The short letter reflects a network of early Christian house churches where traveling teachers depended on hospitality.
books.overall_theme: Christian love must remain joined to truth about Jesus Christ.
books.plain_english_summary: 2 John urges believers to continue in love and obedience but not to provide support to deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

major_events_or_movements.title: Walk in Truth and Love
major_events_or_movements.description: The elder rejoices that some are walking in truth and repeats the command to love one another.

major_events_or_movements.title: Warning about Deceivers
major_events_or_movements.description: False teachers who deny Jesus Christ coming in the flesh are identified as dangerous.

major_events_or_movements.title: Hospitality with Discernment
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are warned not to materially assist teachers who undermine the apostolic message.

key_figures.name: The elder
key_figures.description: The writer, traditionally identified with John the apostle.

key_figures.name: The elect lady and her children
key_figures.description: The recipients, possibly a woman and her household or a local church.

key_figures.name: The deceivers
key_figures.description: Teachers who deny Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.

books.interpretive_notes: Interpreters differ on whether the 'elect lady' is an individual woman or a figurative name for a local church; the warning about hospitality concerns supporting false teachers, not refusing basic kindness.

books.name: 3 John
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Written by 'the elder,' traditionally associated with John the apostle.
books.original_audience: Gaius, a Christian believer known for hospitality.
books.purpose: To commend faithful hospitality, criticize Diotrephes' controlling behavior, and recommend Demetrius.
books.historical_context: The letter reflects early house-church networks in which traveling Christian workers depended on local hospitality and personal trust.
books.overall_theme: Faithful Christian leadership is hospitable, truthful, and humble rather than controlling or self-promoting.
books.plain_english_summary: 3 John praises Gaius for supporting Christian workers, condemns Diotrephes for rejecting authority and hospitality, and commends Demetrius as trustworthy.

major_events_or_movements.title: Gaius Commended
major_events_or_movements.description: Gaius is praised for walking in truth and supporting traveling believers.

major_events_or_movements.title: Diotrephes Rebuked
major_events_or_movements.description: A local leader is criticized for loving prominence, rejecting the elder's authority, and blocking hospitality.

major_events_or_movements.title: Demetrius Recommended
major_events_or_movements.description: Demetrius receives a strong recommendation as someone with a good testimony.

key_figures.name: The elder
key_figures.description: The writer, traditionally identified with John the apostle.

key_figures.name: Gaius
key_figures.description: A beloved believer commended for faithful hospitality.

key_figures.name: Diotrephes
key_figures.description: A church leader who loves to be first and refuses to welcome others.

key_figures.name: Demetrius
key_figures.description: Recommended as someone well spoken of by everyone.

books.interpretive_notes: 3 John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count; it offers a rare glimpse into early church conflict over authority and hospitality.

books.name: Jude
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: Jude identifies himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James; traditionally understood as a brother of Jesus.
books.original_audience: Christians threatened by corrupt teachers within the community.
books.purpose: To urge believers to contend for the faith against teachers who distort grace into moral license and reject rightful authority.
books.historical_context: The letter draws heavily on Jewish scriptural and traditional examples familiar to its audience.
books.overall_theme: God's people must defend the apostolic faith, resist corrupt teaching, and persevere in God's love while showing mercy wisely.
books.plain_english_summary: Jude changes from an intended letter about shared salvation to an urgent warning about infiltrating teachers. It combines severe judgment examples with practical instructions for perseverance and mercy.

major_events_or_movements.title: Call to Contend for the Faith
major_events_or_movements.description: Jude urges believers to defend the faith because corrupt teachers have entered the community.

major_events_or_movements.title: Examples of Judgment
major_events_or_movements.description: Israel in the wilderness, rebellious angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah are invoked as warnings.

major_events_or_movements.title: Persevere and Show Mercy
major_events_or_movements.description: Believers are told to build themselves up, pray, remain in God's love, and rescue others with discernment.

key_figures.name: Jude
key_figures.description: A servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James.

key_figures.name: Michael the archangel
key_figures.description: Cited as one who would not slander even the devil, leaving judgment to the Lord.

key_figures.name: Enoch
key_figures.description: Quoted as prophesying the Lord's coming judgment on the ungodly.

key_figures.name: Cain, Balaam, and Korah
key_figures.description: Examples of rebellion and greed that the false teachers follow.

books.interpretive_notes: Jude quotes or alludes to Jewish traditional writings not included in the Protestant Old Testament. Traditions differ on how to understand the authority of those source materials.

books.name: Revelation
books.traditional_author_or_attribution: John, exiled on Patmos; traditionally identified as John the apostle, though the precise identity is debated.
books.original_audience: Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, with a wider message for the church.
books.purpose: To reveal Jesus Christ as sovereign Lord, strengthen believers under pressure, warn compromised churches, and promise God's final victory over evil.
books.historical_context: Revelation emerges from the Roman imperial world, where churches faced pressure to accommodate idolatry, emperor-centered civic religion, persecution, and economic compromise.
books.overall_theme: Jesus reigns, evil will be judged, faithful witness matters, and God will ultimately renew creation and dwell with His people.
books.plain_english_summary: Revelation uses vivid apocalyptic symbols, letters, visions, hymns, judgments, and final renewal imagery. It calls churches to faithful witness while assuring them that God, not empire or evil, has the final word.

major_events_or_movements.title: Messages to the Seven Churches
major_events_or_movements.description: Jesus commends, warns, and calls seven churches to perseverance and repentance.

major_events_or_movements.title: Conflict, Judgment, and Faithful Witness
major_events_or_movements.description: Heavenly worship, seals, trumpets, beasts, Babylon, and bowls portray the cosmic conflict between God's kingdom and rebellious powers.

major_events_or_movements.title: Final Victory and New Creation
major_events_or_movements.description: Christ triumphs, evil is judged, and a new heaven and new earth culminate in God's dwelling with humanity.

key_figures.name: Jesus
key_figures.description: The risen Christ, the Lamb who was slain, the faithful witness, and the King of kings.

key_figures.name: John
key_figures.description: Receives the revelation while exiled on the island of Patmos.

key_figures.name: Antipas
key_figures.description: A faithful witness put to death in Pergamum.

key_figures.name: 'Jezebel'
key_figures.description: A self-proclaimed prophetess in Thyatira who leads believers into compromise.

key_figures.name: The two witnesses
key_figures.description: Prophetic figures who testify, are killed, and are raised by God.

key_figures.name: The woman and the dragon
key_figures.description: A woman clothed with the sun gives birth to a male child; the dragon, Satan, wages war against her and her offspring.

key_figures.name: The beast and the false prophet
key_figures.description: Symbolic powers that demand worship and deceive the earth.

key_figures.name: Babylon the great
key_figures.description: A symbolic city portrayed as a prostitute, representing corrupt worldly power.

key_figures.name: The Bride of the Lamb
key_figures.description: God's people, pictured as the New Jerusalem coming down from heaven.

books.interpretive_notes: Revelation is interpreted through several major frameworks, including futurist, preterist, historicist, and idealist approaches. The book's symbolic visions should not be presented as though one detailed end-times system is universally accepted.
